Any trial progress you make carries over to the full game if you decide to purchase it, and once your five hours are up, that's it - you can't restart the trial on a different save or something like that. The timer is final.

Charting the Unknown is the first bit of DLC for the game - there's likely more to come - and a Switch 2 version of the sandbox fantasy RPG is currently in development. The developer has hinted at multiplayer-focused DLC in the future, as well as a sequel to the popular game. If you're curious what took the world by storm earlier this year, you can try the free trial on your console of choice right now.

Hark, it's a good day - we got slivers of information about The Elder Scrolls 6 from Bethesda. First, the game is actually called The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, which is very nice to know, and we've also learned when it'll be taking place, and it's quite close to predecessor Skyrim.

Bethesda main man Todd Howard made the reveal himself in the studio's new video commemorating its 40th anniversary. Several key games across the company's lifespan were acknowledged, before Howard mentioned we'd learn the title in a short promo clip.

But then afterward came something for the aficionados - a quote from Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes," it reads. "A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate."

It comes from 4E 206. That stands out because it takes place exactly five years after Skyrim. Absent any other context, the year could be significant or just a minor detail.

If, for instance, that's when Sentinel takes place, it's the shortest gap between mainline entries. Skyrim takes place two centuries after Oblivion, which is only six years after Morrowind. The third Elder Scrolls entry is set 22 years after the previous game, and then there's another six-year jump between Daggerfall and Arena.

The fact it's from Hammerfell could be significant. We've only visited the region in Elder Scrolls Online since Daggerfall, creating a certain amount of potential for exploration.

Offhand, there really isn't enough information to say how this matters, leaving lore nerds to ruminate until Bethesda provides another clue in however many years. I'm curious about the use of a Moth Priest here as well. They're scholars of the literal Elder Scrolls, but we don't see them much. Perhaps now we'll go deeper on them and the Ancient Moth. One can only hope. But at least the series timeline just got another little bump.

The Treasure Hunters mini-season has several Gold vehicles you can win in Fortnite, but finding them won’t be easy. They’re part of many goodies you can unlock throughout the course of the season.

Let’s find out all the available models, and more importantly, how you can get them all.

Gold cars are special versions of the ordinary vehicle skins that you can find in the game. They have a bright yellow glimmer, which also makes them pretty rare to find. The only way to find them during the Treasure Hunters season, as of writing, is to open chests.

Gold cars are one of the various rare items that have been added to the regular treasure chest. They are the second-rarest tier of rewards, so the only item that’s harder to find in comparison is the Pirate Shop access token.

Finding one will completely depend on your luck. If the odds are in your favor, you might open one chest and find a gold car. Realistically, however, you will need to open several at minimum to add one to your collection.

You can always increase the luck in your favor by visiting the vaults. Guarantees you four rare chase stoppers, which have enhanced rates for rarer rewards. Similarly, you can also use certain spirit abilities to raise the odds in your favor.

Ultimately, keep opening the chest until you turn out to be lucky. If you are playing in a group, only one of you needs to find the car.

There will be four different models available for you to collect. So far, we are only in Week 1, but there are three more weeks to follow after this one.

Nagoshi Studio revealed Gang of Dragon less than a year ago, but it ran into trouble just a few months later.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Six months after the disappearance of Nagoshi Studio's website, a Google-translated notice in the Japan government's Kanpo website (via Gematsu) says the company has now officially closed its doors.

Founded by Yakuza creator Toshihiro Nagoshi in 2021 after a run of more than 30 years at Sega, Nagoshi Studio's first game was revealed at the 2025 Game Awards as Gang of Dragon—although the reveal was really just a brief CGI clip of Ma Dong-Seok that could have been lifted straight from Korean action film The Outlaws.

The wheels came off just a few months later, though, when NetEase pulled funding for the studio, amidst a broader pullback from external studio support over the previous year. Nagoshi Studio reportedly had no success finding another benefactor to fill the gap, and two months later, in May, the studio's website disappeared.

No official proclamations about the fate of the studio were forthcoming, though, and the Steam page remained online, so faint hope of a last-minute rescue persisted. Now, I'm afraid even that's gone, although the Steam listing is still up if you want to poke around at what might have been.

#3796. Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3's online servers are temporarily going dark, FromSoftware announces

Things might get even darker over in the world of Lordran without those silly, only sometimes helpful notes left by other players. Developer FromSoftware has announced that it's temporarily closing Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 servers because of an unspecified issue.

"Due to a server issue, the game servers for the following titles will be temporarily unavailable on all platforms," the RPG studio tweeted earlier today, before naming Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3.

While the server shutdown won't last forever, FromSoftware hasn't told series fans when exactly they can expect online play to be restored. That presumably means PvP invasions, summon signs and in-game messages that try to troll you off a cliff are unavailable for the time being.

"We will provide updates once we have information regarding the server restoration time. We apologize for the inconvenience," the studio added. I hope you've stocked up on Estus Flasks, at least.

Of course, this isn't the first time the Dark Souls trilogy has had to contend with server problems. In 2022, Bandai Namco took servers for all three Dark Souls games offline due to a security vulnerability affecting Dark Souls 3. The threequel went dark once again a few months later.

FromSoftware's next game The Duskbloods - the one with the jetpacks and vampires and a cute bird thing - hasn't been any luckier, either. The multiplayer-focused game's first network test had to be taken offline early due to similarly vague "server issues". More recently, FromSoftware delayed its Switch 2 exclusive into next year.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," the developer tweeted this week. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

#3795. Developers, Creators, And Fans Remember BioWare: ‘I’ve Been Trying To Replicate That Feeling For Almost My Whole Life’

When I initially put out a call for fans, developers, creators, and media to reach out to me with stories about their experiences with BioWare, the now-shuttered developer of some of the most beloved western RPGs of the past 30 years, I was frankly overwhelmed by the outpouring of responses from people who had a story to tell. I was so overwhelmed, in fact, that I was only able to use a fraction of what showed up in my inbox for this collection of memories, praise, righteous anger, and mourning. Whether they were old heads who had been playing BioWare games since the days of Shattered Steel and the original Baldurâs Gate or folks who fell in love with the Edmonton studioâs work through Mass Effect and Dragon Age, itâs clear that BioWareâs games left an imprint on fans that has outlived the company itself.

(Submissions have been lightly edited for style and clarity.)

If BioWareâs games have proven anything, itâs that everyoneâs story has its own unique beginning, and thatâs reflected in how its fans came to know its work through so many different points of entry.

My first BioWare experience was with the first two Baldur’s Gate games. I wasn’t much of a PC CRPG gamer in 1998 but BG1 just absolutely blew me away with what, at the time, felt like endless options for character customization, the broad sweep of the story that felt like a true investment in the Dungeons & Dragons tabletop I had been playing for only a few years at that point – and the Forgotten Realms where I cut my teeth as both player and Dungeon Master – and the amazing writing on the characters. This doubled in effect when BG2 arrived in the year 2000, and between those two games I lived in BioWare’s Forgotten Realms like it was a second home. â Phil Morgan, host of Deleted Saves Podcast

I swiped Baldur’s Gate from my dad when I was nine – he wasn’t into role-playing games and I have no idea why he had it, but it clicked immediately for me and I spent hours trying different types of characters, killing NPCs I shouldn’t have, and getting to know that world. It blew me away when I realized I could recruit different party members in Baldur’s Gate, and that it had an impact on the story. It meant I could replay the game over and over and make different choices to see what would happen, and that became something BioWare was known for. â Chuck Zimmerheld, Giant Bomb

Years [after playing KOTOR], my next experience was attending a Video Games Live concert with conductor Jack Wall, who was the composer for the first two Mass Effect games, and that’s where I first heard the Mass Effect theme. That song was so beautiful to me that I knew I had to play the game it had come from. I didn’t have a lot of money at the time, but I scrimped and saved and got my brother to go half in with me on an Xbox 360. I bought a used copy of Mass Effect before we’d even gotten the Xbox, I was so excited. It blew my mind AGAIN in so many ways. A shooter RPG. A unique space adventure not tied to the IPs I’d enjoyed all my life. I fell in love with all of the unique characters and the idea of a space-faring future where humans weren’t the dominant species felt so fresh and exciting. â Jeremy Greco, BioWare fan

My first experience with BioWare, and one of my earliest memories of gaming in general, was watching my older brother play Dragon Age: Origins in 2010 on our PS3. I was frankly terrified watching it as an 8 year old. To this day, seeing the Darkspawn still conjures up a deep-rooted childhood fear of the Blight sweeping across the land. I remember playing through the game a few years later, thinking I was braver, and being absolutely horrified by the Circle Mage origin. I mean the Harrowing was insane to me. I think it took me maybe a week of going back and forth to finally finish that prologue. That game absolutely set the bar for me of dark heroic fantasy and hugely influenced my taste in games and stories ever since. â Jerram Carr, junior narrative designerÂ

BioWareâs games were the origin story for many developersâ own careers. You can trace the influences and inspirations that shaped the work of many designers and writers back to the worlds the company created.

I think the most impactful game for me was Dragon Age: Origins. I was in college excited for a new Bioware game, but at the same time struggling with accepting myself as a gay man. I had the chance to flirt with Alistair as a man, and while he ultimately rejected me, he helped me feel seen; that it was okay to be gay. I remember crying on the floor, moved that a 3D character had given me so much grace to be myself. I remember wanting to make games so people could have moments like I did. Moments to accept ourselves and see ourselves reflected positively.

When I did get the chance to make queer people feel seen in Destiny it felt like I was helping pay back the gift the DA:O team had given me. I even talked about it in the Bungie weekly blog.Â  â Nigel Davis, senior producer at Entangled Publishing, formerly at Bungie

The creators at BioWare pushed the industry forward with player choice in games. Optional party members, loyalty quests, morality systems, and huge choices with multi-game impacts. RPG’s aren’t the same without them. â Chuck Zimmerheld, Giant Bomb

Few studios can say that they changed the way genres are made. BioWare can. Thereâs an entire generation of developers and narrative designers that work in the industry because they were inspired by the games BioWare made across a 30-year run that largely produced classic after classic after classic. The systems the folks at BioWare designed worked their ways into other games in ways that you could see and interact with. My buddies and I used to joke that BioWare invented the wheel because Mass Effectâs dialogue wheel felt like it was everywhere after the original game was released. â Will Borger, journalist and consultant

For me, it all traces back to those first two Baldur’s Gate games. There’s a direct line from those to my work today, including my writing on Pacific Drive, where I’ve tried to remember to highlight the everyday as well as the extraordinary, to add jokes as well as drama, to imagine how even the smallest details shape the most fantastical world. And when she got to her final glory, no, it wasn’t some cutscene cavalcade of sins remembered flashing before my eyes. It was me, and just me, holding the controller, considering everything I had done to and for this galaxy, and being asked to make a judgement call. And that judgement call, unlike any other game I had ever playedâand extremely few sinceâwas to choose peace. To choose evolution. To share. To Synthesize. And for Shepard to rest.

Before they even added the extended endings, I remember sitting there, thinking of what kind of universe Shepard would never get to see. And, seemingly unlike the rest of the internet, I was content. â Justin Clark, games media

The introduction of Steve Cortez. I think that was still my first experience with a game that gave me [a gay romance] option, and certainly the first one that wasn’t giving that option in a way that stank of “oh look at how progressive we are being, aren’t we amazing?!” At the time it was at least a year before gay marriage became legal in the UK, and so it felt significant. Since then BioWare has been a studio that I associate with telling stories over trying to fit in with what the rest of the AAA competition was doing at the time. â Gabe Titchiner, BioWare fan

I played Mass Effect for the first time when I was a teenager. Things weren’t great at home. I had just come out as a lesbian and my family didn’t accept it. I was struggling to find acceptance and community. Mass Effect provided that to me. Playing through an incredibly well-written sapphic romance spanning three whole games gave me a sense of belonging at a crucial time in my life. Commander Shepard became my role model. I found the Mass Effect community online and developed friendships in it that have lasted over a decade. Those games and the friendships I found through them changed me forever. â Sage, BioWare fan

I think [what impressed me the most] was how Dragon Age II subverted the expectation of player agency. This wasnât Mass Effect, or Origins, or KOTOR where the right selection of choices could save the world. Your world was going to hell no matter what. You just got to choose what kind of person you wanted to be while your life burned down around you.

The game thereby became an altogether more intimate tale of a found family caught in the tide of history. The cast of violent, sexually fluid weirdos remains one of the all-time great RPG parties, and the deeply cursed city of Kirkwall is an all-time great fantasy setting. With a narrative that spans years, you get to feel like you havenât just gone on adventure: youâve built a life for yourself and your friends. When you must choose who to side with at the end of the game, whether to side with the inevitability of authority or with the chaos of rebellion, that moment carries a weight that most RPGs canât match, precisely because the game has spent its efforts investing you in the characters and the setting, not just the plot.

I donât give a good goddamn what people say about it: for my money, Dragon Age II is one of the greatest video games ever made. It challenged my beliefs about what made a good narrative, and that made me a better author and critic. â Saoirse Stone BioWare fan, critic, author, Editor-In-Chief at Stone Freedom

The twist in KotOR was my âI am your father.â It completely got me and Iâve been trying to replicate that feeling for almost my whole life. â Eric Perez, BioWare fan

The Revealâ¢ in KOTOR is legendary, but even outside that, you could already see that this studio was special in the way it could build a universe for you. Learning the ancient history of the sand people hit me in the way the best epic fantasy and science fiction does. […] Whoever wrote and animated the bit in Mass Effect 2 where youâre sneaking onto a Geth station and Joker notes that their stealth systems just hide emissions and anyone could see the Normandy by looking out a window, and Legion explains that windows are illogical while Joker silently makes a robot face and robot arms gestures? I love you. Top five video game jokes of all time. â Chase Wheatley, BioWare fan

I used to tell people I hated [Dragon Age II], but I was still compelled by it. I played all the different classes, genders, and personalities, trying to get the shape of the thing. I realize now that DAII was ahead of its time. It was revolutionary in the way the characters developed and changed over time, reacting to the events in Kirkwall because of their pasts in ways I couldnât predict.Â  â Shayna Moon, senior technical director

The moment in BG1 that I stepped outside of Candlekeep in the prologue was just… It was a moment I’ll never forget. For the first time, I was THERE. BioWare had provided for me a moment of discovery that had previously only existed at the nexus of character sheets, graph paper and dice. And seconds later when Elminster arrived with his classic red attire and the line “Ho there, wanderer…”, that has created a moment that has stayed with me for almost 30 years. â Phil Morgan, host of Deleted Saves Podcast

I remember the first time I played through Mass Effect as a teenager, and feeling the floor dropping out from under me. Towards the end of the game you meet Vigil, a virtual intelligence of the Prothean race. Vigil explains how everything we’ve been doing, every battle against the Geth that we’ve been fighting, has all been just another turn in a long cycle perpetuated by the Reapers, and it felt like getting hit by a bag of bricks. A massive chasm had opened up before me and I felt this immenseness to the world and story that I was just seeing the tiniest glimpse into. I was completely enthralled afterwards. It was genuinely magic. A mystical moment for me. â- Jerram Carr, junior narrative designer

The Suicide Mission in Mass Effect 2 is one of the greatest achievements in the medium. It culminated in choices [that were] impactful, relevant, and personal without feeling contrived. Some things you learn to appreciate; others, like this, you know are legendary the moment you encounter them. â Colin Mancini, TTRPG designer

The moment that sticks with me is the night I beat Dragon Age II. It was during finals, so I was already taking time away from studying to mainline this game. I hit the credits and that beautiful orchestrated version of “I’m Not Calling You a Liar” by Florence and the Machine and I remember sitting on my uncomfortable couch in my otherwise empty dorm living room and feeling this incredible sense of accomplishment and loss and connection. Someone had made this for me and I’d played it and loved it and now it was over, and the world felt a little bit different. â Aysha U. Farah, narrative designer

There’s so many moments in BioWare’s games that felt impactful to me, but if I had to narrow it down to one it would definitely be Dorian facing off with his father in Inquisition. I had never seen a major, AAA game cover a topic as hard and real as conversion therapy like that. It was an act of incredible bravery on David Gaider and the whole writing team’s part to put that in and left a major impact on me as a queer fan. From that moment on I knew I felt safe and seen in BioWare’s games, and it’s why I’ve returned to their games over and over again to find some manner of safety and solace in a world that keeps taking it from us LGBTQ+ folks bit by bit. â Brendan, BioWare fan

I found that usually when I played create-your-own-character RPGs, I’d try to create characters mostly reflective of myself. But with BioWare games, I started to not do that anymore. I started to make characters no longer tied to myself like that. I gave them their own personalities, designs and instead of asking, “What would I do?” when it came to making a choice, I started asking, “What would my Warden do?” or “What would my Shepard do?” Because of this, I’d spend hours in character creation, going over the choices in their games to fine-tune which ones my characters would make and why. How it would suit them. BioWare gives you a backstory to work with and the rest is yours to play with. And because I’d spend so much time thinking about these intricacies, I began to realize BioWare was helping me learn things about storytelling and character design.

I could only do this because BioWare gave me the tools and I will forever be grateful for them for it, for it taught me things and allowed me to enjoy things I’ve rarely gotten from a developer of any other video game. It showed me how to love and appreciate story and the characters in them in a way I hadn’t previously. â AzzieSky, BioWare fan

The big twist in [KOTOR] gets talked about a lot. But, for me, the thing that really comes to mind is saving the character Juhani on my second playthrough. Youâre training to be a Jedi who does good, Jedi things; they tell you to go find some tainted grove on Dantooine and cleanse it. Juhani is a young Cathar Jediâprobably the first explicitly queer character in all of Star Wars, by the wayâwho has fallen to the dark side. She took a lightsaber to her own master during training, and now she feels lost and unwilling to return to the Jedi Enclave. You, as the player, get to decide how to handle this: you choose your words wisely and hope sheâll listen to reason. And the first time, I failed to get through to her, and I had to cut her down in battle. On my second run, though, I talked some sense into her, and she became my Jedi companion through the rest of the story. Sheâs a rich character, and I hadnât even realized she was a possible ally the first time. Iâd simply killed her. But her redemption arc is really beautiful, especially when you learn that her master ultimately survived. â Alex James Kane, writer and YouTuber

To this day, I donât think Iâve ever been as emotionally immersed in a scene as the late-game DAII quest when Varric confronts his traitorous brother. The game gives the player a say in whether Varric should kill him or let him live, and as with so many BioWare game decisions, there isnât an obvious right or wrong answer. But in that moment, I wasnât a player trying to determine right or wrong. I was Hawke, last of her line, begging Varric not to sacrifice the only sibling he had. And I had no idea whether heâd listen to meânot because I didnât trust the game to give me agency, but because I trusted the game to give Varric the agency to do whatever was truest to his character. â Charlotte Reber, she/her, fan and author of Dragon Age II from Boss Fight Books

BioWare has been gutted by EA repeatedly over the course of its life, and as a result, many of the people who made the studioâs greatest games were already gone by the time it closed. But even in those final months, people who had been involved in games like the original Mass Effect trilogy were working on the game that would have been Mass Effect: Universe. Now that the entire team is scattered to the winds, its legacy still remains, and wherever they go on to create games now, hopefully weâll see the studioâs DNA in whatever comes next.

I hope the folks who worked at Bioware know that, across several games, they let me dream, not just of strange new worlds, but better worlds, when we needed them most. I cannot thank them enough for that. â Justin Clark, games media

I’d hope everyone who helped bring the games to us knows that they helped me learn so much about myself, and how I think about things. Like realizing I’m Ace-leaning because of Bellara’s romance. Or how much of my attitude towards life was shaped by Varric, Sera, Iron Bull (“people are just people”) and their takes on things. There’s so much more I can say, but I just hope they know I’m forever grateful. â @LavaCastle, BioWare fan

Funnily enough I don’t have any particular hopes about what BioWare’s developers think of the legacy they left behind, because the groundswell of support that happened in the last 24 hours has probably reached most all of them (it’s certainly more than I was expecting from the internet given the tones in which BioWare has been discussed in modern videogame discourse). I think even the ones that have deliberately cut themselves off from the community (understandably, in some instances) know they are loved, they are appreciated, and are responsible for some of the most formative storytelling experiences in the medium amongst their peers beyond even that of the RPG genre. I suppose I hope they know that they and their stories are worth their weight in gold, and no amount of braying from culture warriors and armchair developers will ever change that. â Jeff, BioWare fan and The Last Staunch Defender of Anthem On The Planet

I hope they know just how powerful they made their worlds. From Garrus and each character you could impact in Mass Effect 2, to the way they carved out a special place for a character’s emotions to simply be. I felt like taking your time in these games and experiencing the characters’ stories was the goal.Â

I hope they all also know how loved they all are. Not just for the things they created, but for the way they approached the human condition in all their games so eloquently. BioWare, thank you. We see you, and we love you for your humanity imprinted in the stories you told. â Arielle Danan, journalist and freelance video editor at IGN

The organization may be gone, but the stories they told and worlds they created will live on forever in the hearts of the countless people their stories touched. ClichÃ©, but true. BioWare will forever be a name that means exceptional and significant RPGs, but it’s the people and developers behind that name that made that impact. â Winter, BioWare fan

It’s actually surprised me how much the news of BioWare’s final end has taken me out. Everyone knows it’s been a shambling corpse for years, arguably since the doctors left, but especiallyâas my spouse points outâsince longtime writer Mary Kirby was turfed. It’s been pulled in so many stupid directions by the C-suite and not really had a proper identity in years.

When I discovered KOTOR, and first learned it was made in my home province of Alberta, I was stunned. I didn’t know we had a games industry. That stuff happened in Japan and L.A. and places like that, not Edmonton. Edmonton was the frozen wasteland where hockey players got underpaid in Canadian money until they were free to go south for the real dough. But, no, here was a big-name game studio trying to do more interesting things (especially for the time) with story, character, and even sex in games. Sure, we know now that BioWare was never the progressive paradise it liked to portray itself as, but at the time it felt like a counter to all the fuckass conservatives in my homeland, the oil barons and the ranching yokels. And the Easter eggs! They were for me! The Athabasca-class freighters in Mass Effect were named for Lake Athabasca in northern Alberta (and Saskatchewan). I knew that! That was for me! I was being winked at by big-name game developers!

It feels like an old friend I’d drifted away from over the years has been taken off life support. Sure, things were never going to be what they once were, and no, living on this way obviously isn’t what they would’ve wanted, but it’s still a day of grief and shock in spite of everything. â Doogie, BioWare fan

I hope all the devs know that their work mattered. It mattered so, so much. They put out quality work in a genre space that both elevated narrative expectations for the medium and offered a lifeline to a lot of scared, lonely queer kids. â Saoirse Stone, BioWare fan, critic, author, Editor-In-Chief at Stone Freedom

I hope you know that you all deserved better. I love the worlds you created, and you all deserve to keep creating in them. You deserve to get to try again after a misstep. You deserve recognition for your impact on the industry and on your fans. You deserve all the money currently filling the pockets of people who already have too much and who will continue to profit off the IPs you created. You deserve to keep doing what you love. I wish you all the best. â Chase Wheatley, BioWare fan

If there’s one thing I’m certain of, it’s that BioWare will live on, in some fashion, in the hearts of its fans. We’re too passionate, and strange, and wonderful to let it all go just because some money-hungry fascists think that art is something they can own and kill. BioWare belongs to the community now. Dragon Age and Mass Effect belong to the artists, and writers, and weirdos, and outcasts. To the queers, both baby and late-in-life. I don’t know what happens with the developers and the worlds, but I do know that we won’t let them die. The things Bioware made matter too much for that to happen. I want the developers to know that. That what they did mattered to us, and we won’t abandon that trust just because the studio is gone. â Christine Joy Sonneault, writer

[Ex-BioWare writer] Sam Maggs once described BioWare as âthe best narrative studio in the world,â and Iâd like to think all the folks who have been a part of it knew, on some level, they had really achieved that. We have CD Projekt and some other really great interactive storytelling now, but when Knights of the Old Republic and Mass Effect arrived on the scene, there was nothing else with that level of ambition, and they managed to really rise to it. The first Dragon Age feels a lot like Peter Jacksonâs Lord of the Rings trilogy to me, in that sense. The medium bends and strains under all this talent, and wanting the narrative to have all this branching, with full voice-over and lifelike in-engine facial animation. Plus, your created character gets to be present within all of those cinematic moments. They did a lot of things first, they connected with players on a level most game studios simply donât, and they delivered a really beautiful game in Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which Iâll forever cherish as their return-to-form moment. â Alex James Kane, writer and YouTuber

What makes me sad is seeing so many people saying that MASS EFFECT IS DEAD and…I disagree. That’s not how art works. Mass Effect is art, and art is eternal. Art transcends its creator and eventually begins to belong to the people who experience it. That’s precisely why I chose the name We Are Mass Effect for my project. Mass Effect will continue to live on as long as people talk about the series, quote its dialogue, create fan art, or simply recommend it to someone else, allowing that cycle to begin all over again.

Of course, I understand that when people talk about its death, they’re mostly referring to the franchise itself. We might never get another Mass Effect game, but that honestly doesn’t matter to me. In fact, I hate the capitalist dynamics of franchise culture, where a work’s name has to be exploited endlessly until its legacy is completely diluted into a collection of mediocre, artificial products orbiting around the original masterpiece that started it all.Â

Don’t get me wrong, I’m only human, and of course I was excited to see what Michael Gamble and the rest of the team were planning for the next Mass Effect. But from a more spiritual perspective, none of this really changes anything for me, apart from my concern for all the unfortunate people who now have to leave their jobs. And that’s why, to me, Mass Effect is alive, and it always will be. Because Mass Effect is art, and art is eternal. â Ariel, creator of the We Are Mass Effect project

The Lord of the Rings and Star Wars sparked my interest in high fantasy and science fiction, but BioWare turned them into lifelong series I’d follow for most of my life. I may never experience a Mass Effect or Dragon Age narrative again, and that is really unfortunate. â Jerrad Wyche, Controlled Interests

I hope that all the development team members, wherever they’ve gone between then and now, know that BioWare games have saved lives. They’ve influenced how I write, draw, and play around in my own creative universes. These are games and characters that have become fondly remembered defining moments in several decades of my life. I honestly don’t know how I would have reacted to several life events if Dragon Age games and Mass Effect games weren’t lodged in my brain and hadnât provided me with some very happy memories. â Andrew Fedge, BioWare fan

Grief is often more than just sadness, as there can be anger mixed in there as well. BioWareâs closure, coming two months after the private equity conglomerate made up of Saudi Arabia Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake Partners, and Trump son-in-law Jared Kushnerâs Affinity Partners acquired Electronic Arts for $55 billion, is violent cultural vandalism, and whether you liked the studioâs later output or not, itâs fine to call a spade a spade.

Beyond feeling sad for BioWare âthe studio” for shutting down, I am especially sad for the real people who made BioWare what it is: all of the employees who lost their jobs because of (in my opinion) idiotic business decisions from way higher up. It angers me that the creatives who spend so much time and energy putting their hearts and souls into their work to invent these immersive worlds for us to experience are being treated so poorly, and I sincerely hope we get a “reboot” on the entire video game industry in the future. â Niema Moshiri, Associate Teaching Professor of Computer Science & Engineering, UC San Diego

Can I say fuck EA? If so, fuck EA, fuck Jared Kushner, fuck private equity. If not, then Iâd like to say that I hope that if the Mass Effect show comes out and is successful like Fallout then I hope the executives are raked over the coals for making such a short-sighted decision. â Taylor, BioWare fan

It’s going to be a process but I know eventually I’ll be able to make peace with the fact that BioWare is no longer with us. Despite everything, they had an incredible run of games that left such an impact on millions of LGBTQ+ gamers like myself, and that is something that can NEVER be taken away no matter what bloodless skinsuit holds the rights to their IP now. Legendary BioWare creatives like Mike Laidlaw, Mark Darrah, David Gaider, Casey Hudson, and Karin and Trick Weekes just to name a few are out making their own games and projects again and I can’t wait to play them. I’m choosing to see the light at the end of this tunnel and recognize that while BioWare the company may be gone, BioWare the community, the games, the art, and the talent will live on and there’s not a single fucking thing Jared Kushner or Mohammed bin Salman or any of their underlings at EA can do about it. â Brendan, BioWare fan

For anyone who has ever doubted that video games are political, I am asking you to look at the chain of events that led to this closure and realize that a lack of federal financial regulation is the reason that this happened, along with bold-faced corruption from the Trump administration. Entertainment is made by people, and right now if you play video games, the people making your entertainment are suffering. Iâm one of the lucky ones whoâs currently employed, but every day I feel the strain of just how many of my friends and developers I look up to are currently out of work or suffering on teams that donât properly value them. Learn the history of labor organizing and recognize that the way we get great games like BioWareâs is to have strong, stable teams that are allowed to do their jobs without the interference of a corporate rat like Andrew Wilson or Jared Kushner. â Shayna Moon, senior technical director

Itâs not like words could ever convey how much BioWareâs gamesâMass Effect and Dragon Age in particularâmean to me. Language is not built to capture feelings like this; itâs both a tragedy and what makes life beautiful.

And I wouldnât be living this life without those games. I mean that quite literally. Mass Effect helped me during the most difficult period of my life as a teenager, and Dragon Age inspired me to dream. In the last ten years, Iâve been many things: game journalist, game design consultant, PR specialist, community manager, social media manager, marketing consultant. Writer and narrative designer. This industry does not deserve us dreaming that our lives will be intertwined with it, but nonethelessâ¦I still dream of writing games for a living.Â

Iâve accomplished almost every major dream Iâve had in my life thus far. I can trace this ambition directly back to that first time I experienced Mass Effect 3 and Dragon Age: Inquisition. It feels fitting, then, that my dream of working at BioWare someday is the one dream that got away. My heart is shattered and grateful in equal measure. What a damned industry. What incredible dreamers whose creations will outlive whatever remains of this industry.Â

As Shepard once said: âNobody ever fell in love without being a little brave.â Thank you to every person at BioWare who made those games with kindness, creativity, and hope despite the ever-difficult circumstances. I think experiencing their work was the first time I ever fell in love, and that love makes me a little more brave every day.Â

It had to be them. Someone else might have gotten it wrong. â Natalie Checo, game writer and marketing specialist

Dragon Age IIâs story isnât precisely a classical tragedy, but it does follow a tragic arc: a hero who loses everything, rises back up, becomes a championâand then loses it all, not to hubris, but to hostile forces beyond their control, leaving them stranded once again in a world where hope is tenuous and the future deeply uncertain. That doesnât mean Hawke failed, or that everything they did was pointless. They did so much good along the way. They changed lives, saved lives, laughed and wept and fought and loved, and made the world a better place for it.

Thatâs the BioWare story. And like all BioWare stories, itâs a pretty damn good one. Thank you for letting us join the party and fight at your side. â Charlotte Reber, she/her, fan and author of Dragon Age II from Boss Fight Books

#3794. The Division 2 Y8S3 Red Horizon Week 11 Manhunt HVT: Scout 11 solutions

The Division 2 Y8S3 Red Horizon Week 11 is now live, and we can immediately access this season’s Climax mission. There are three tasks to complete as usual, and things aren’t looking too difficult in Week 11. However, there’s a HVT mission to complete before we can get the Exotic.

Once again, you’ll have to use the clues for the first task to complete it. This will reveal what needs to be done for the next one (and then the last one). In this guide, I have decoded all three clues, so you know what has to be done to access the Climax mission.

Living World Activities represent all the random stuff happening in the background. For this task, you’ll need to finish any three of them, at any difficulty of your liking. However, they must belong to the Black Tusk faction to qualify. My preferences are shorter events like Hostage Rescue and Public Executions since they take less time.

Invaded mission refers to the Black Tusk version of ordinary missions. You’ll get to make this switch before starting a fresh mission from the menu. To finish this task, you’ll also need to finish Tidal Basin first so that you’re in Tier 5.

The easiest way to locate these missions is by seeing the red-colored hexagon pattern that replaces the traditional grey one.

Finally, the bounty will be available once you clear the first two tasks. The location can be found on the map itself, and you’ll get 15 minutes to activate it. Then, you can begin the assault to complete the bounty. The mission is straightforward if you have done it as part of the main campaign.

Once you eliminate all the enemies, Higgins will appear in his special gear. Take him down, and you’ll complete the final task. You have to finish all three HVT hunts to take part in the climax mission.

15 years after remaking the game for 3DS purely to "do something about the water temple"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Zelda series lead Eiji Aonuma has admitted that he wanted to use The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake to make the Water Temple a bit less obtuse.

In the 28 years since The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, one challenge has lived in infamy: the dreaded Water Temple. While the classic adventure game was universally praised, the Water Temple was the sole sticking point for many, with its somewhat obtuse design proving a huge challenge. However, to many people – myself included – the problem with the Water Temple was less about the challenge or dungeon design itself and more about the tedium of constantly pausing to equip or remove the Iron Boots to navigate the area.

As for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, Aonuma – whose role in the N64 classic was as the game's dungeon designer – explained that the Water Temple was a big motivator in Nintendo's Ask the Developer article about the game. "I had some overdue homework: I wanted to do something about the Water Temple I created 28 years ago," Aonuma says, explaining, "Since it became well known for its difficulty in the original game, I had the team make some adjustments in this version."

However, this is not the first time Aonuma spoke about wanting to change the Water Temple; in fact, in a 2011 Iwata Asks interview, Aonuma said, "I wanted to do something about the Water Temple" when discussing his motivation for making The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time 3D. He explained at the time, "Everyone talks about it, so it’s been a longstanding wish of mine these 13 years!" but clearly its version of the dreaded dungeon wasn't enough.

"When I designed the Water Temple all those years ago, I wanted to create an experience where simply being underwater was fun," Aonuma explains in 2026. He cites his love of freediving and finds it fascinating "how different everything feels" when you are submerged.

"I wanted to create a place where players could experience those sensations," Aonuma explains. The remake's director, HokWai Ng, explains that the remake makes item toggling easier, as well as changing "some of the walls that made it easy to lose your sense of direction to lattice-style structures," so hopefully this new version will finally satisfy Aonuma's desire to "fix" the temple.

I went back for more of this farming and restauranting sim after downloading its demo during Steam Next Fest. I really enjoy how the serving duties ramp up with custom orders and customer patience after the first few days and will definitely dip into the full version.

Look, I don't actually know anything about horses. But I have it on good authority from more knowledgeable friends that the care and realism in this management sim make it for horse lovers in the same way Dressmaker was for sewing hobbyists last month, so I need to see what the fuss is.

#3791. Blizzard hints at console ports for World of Warcraft: Forever - "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want"

After more than two decades dominating the PC MMO battlefield, it sounds like Blizzard Entertainment's taking the idea of a World of Warcraft console port more seriously than ever.

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta seems to have been immensely popular with fans of the series. It's a brand new third version of the iconic multiplayer game that sits alongside WoW's Classic and Retail portions, and it's recaptured many a lapsed Warcraft sicko with tons of good changes, big and small - one of which is controller support for the first time ever.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the decision to keep World of Warcraft: Forever exclusive to PC players, despite now supporting gamepads, vice president and executive producer Holly Longdale hinted that the fantasy game might just make its way to even more devices and players over time.

"What you just described is really what we're after," she told the outlet. "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want. But the first leg of that journey is getting gamepads working really well with World of Warcraft, and we thought Forever was the perfect place to start."

Longdale reckons all gaming platforms might become "more ubiquitous" in the future, as well. She specifically named the Xbox Project Helix, which is said to be a PC-console hybrid device of some kind. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed the next-gen console can even play your PC games earlier in the year.

"Honestly, we just want to be able to play it anywhere. We've seen people getting it working on the ROG Ally X," Longdale added. "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

World of Warcraft: Forever properly launches on the 4th of November.

Despite struggles in the rest of the Xbox division, Forever's beta was supposedly the "largest" in series history. Elsewhere, Longdale acknowledged that some of the developer's decisions won't make everybody equally happy: "I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"

#3789. South Of Midnight Director Says He Doesn’t Think Xbox Should Have Funded It

Now free to pursue its own destiny independent of Xbox, South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games has been actively looking for collaborative work with other partners. But given some comments recently made by creative director David Sears, I wouldn’t be surprised if Compulsion’s next project was something very, very different from South of Midnight; after all, Sears doesn’t think that game was a great business decision to begin with.

In an interview with MinnMax‘s Ben Hanson, Sears speaks at length about Xbox’s decision to fund games like South of Midnight and Double Fine’s Keeper, games which he and Xbox knew would probably not make lots of money (and in fact did not) but would increase Xbox’s prestige, or serve as cultural cornerstones for generations to come. However, he also says that he told people during development, “Somebody is going to say, one day, ‘The money tap, we’re closing those floodgates.’ And that’s going to have really traumatic results downstream.”

Hanson then summarizes what he thinks Sears is saying. “So the idea is, you’re thankful that Microsoft supported the hell out of South of Midnight…but you would not have funded it yourself?”

Sears replied, “Yeah, probably.” He continued:

I wanted to make it. No doubt. Obviously. Because we made it. Would I have turned off someone else’s money flow before South of Midnight? Yeah. Because I’m not completely selfless. It just seems like, in hindsight at least, it was unsustainable. Of course it was going to have a “shocking” outcome. It’s easy to dissect it now. But at the time, I would talk to other directors and [they’d] be like, “How is this happening? How did we get so lucky? Is this a golden era?” And I’d always be like (he sucks in air through his teeth) “For now.” And there’s always a night when Rome burns. I didn’t know exactly when it would be, but I was always worried about it.

Sears concludes this thought by remarking that the Microsoft of today is much “more humane” than the company he knew in the ’90s, as demonstrated by the fact that it let studios spin off in the first place instead of just shutting them down entirely.

In addition to South of Midnight, Compulsion Games is also known for 2018’s We Happy Few, which it made with Gearbox Publishing. It was acquired by Microsoft just ahead of that release to join Xbox Game Studios, and began working on South of Midnight, which was nominated for and won numerous awards after its launch in 2025, including a BAFTA. Compulsion was spun out from Microsoft as a part of Xbox’s recent restructuring, taking with it all its IP and an unknown amount of financial runway. It’s currently unknown whether or not the studio has signed a new project yet.

After 28 long years, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is finally getting a jump button in the Switch 2 remake because Nintendo knew it'd feel "jarring" without one, even if the decision threw some devs from the OG since it was such a "convenient" design choice previously.

Speaking in a new installment of Nintendo's Ask the Developer interview, Ocarina of Time remake program director Hiroki Taguchi – who first joined the Zelda team to work on Breath of the Wild – notes that certain "adjustments" have been made "so that people who've played titles from The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild onward won't find the experience jarring as they make their way through the adventure."

Director HokWai Ng adds to this, specifying that "that's also one of the reasons we removed auto-jump." Previously, Link couldn't jump on command – if push came to shove, he could muster up a hop if you pushed the control stick forward in specific places, and as Ng says, "the places where jumping was possible and where it wasn't were clearly defined."

Even so, that may not cut it for players who've gotten used to the more modern Zelda adventures where they can jump around as much as they please. "So, for Link's jump, we carried over the controls from more recent titles in the series and made it possible to jump anywhere with a single button press," Ng adds.

Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma reckons that this addition "makes exploration much more exciting," but adding it was no small feat. "Since there were places where we preferred players not to jump, the auto-jump system was, in some ways, convenient from a development standpoint," he admits.

"If you remove that restriction and make it possible to jump anywhere, you need to anticipate all kinds of player behavior and make corresponding adjustments to the environment. So, at first, we were like, 'Are we sure about this?'" he laughs. "So, even a single change can instantly increase the number of things that need to be reviewed."

The new jump ability was something that Nintendo had to consider when it came to all the terrain in the game – and how both Young and Adult versions of Link would traverse it. Art director Aya Shida notes that since "the distance they can jump differs slightly between the two," it meant that "even when designing a single piece of terrain, it was challenging to find the right balance in terms of making gaps just the right distance to jump across."

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

This also meant a change to Ocarina of Time's returning Jump Attack. Taguchi notes that in the OG game, you could launch a Jump Attack using just one button, whereas the Switch 2 remake uses a Breath of the Wild-style "two-step approach." However, this didn't sit quite right with Aonuma.

"Trouble was, I was so used to the original game's controls that I just couldn't get the hang of it," Aonuma laughs. "When I told the team, 'This just doesn't feel as satisfying as the original Jump Attack,' they added a way to perform it with a single button press."

The devs are aware this is a matter of personal preference, though – fellow producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi notes that he was "more used to jumping first and then attacking," and that "in the end, we implemented both control schemes so that fans of the original game, as well as those who've played The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild but not The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, could have a comfortable experience. That said, neither control scheme gets in the way of the other."

It's a more flexible approach to modern improvements than the devs took with a different – now scrapped –quality-of-life improvement, though. Aonuma noted how he first requested the devs to add Breath of the Wild-style warp points, but later asked them to be removed after he realized that they ruined the "important" moments of discovery during the exploration of the world.

Zelda dev responsible for Ocarina of Time's infamous Water Temple used the remake to atone for his sins: "I had some overdue homework."

#3787. GOTY hopeful Mina the Hollower bought the studio financial stability "for now," while the Shovel Knight devs work on a new 3D game

Yacht Club Games has confirmed that most of its developers are now working on a brand new 3D game (potentially Shovel Knight 3D), after the critically-acclaimed Mina the Hollower did well enough for the team to continue.

Before launching its old-school adventure game earlier this year, Yacht Club described Mina the Hollower as a "make-or-break" moment for the beloved indie studio. A global pandemic and a failed experiment to turn Yacht Club into a multi-project studio had left the developer on thin ice, it seems.

But Mina the Hollower sold well enough to buy the studio more time, according to a new Reddit AMA full of interesting tidbits. Asked if Mina was able to secure financial stability for the company, Sean Velasco simply said "yes… for now!" Mina managed to sell over 500,000 copies in its first two weeks, so it's well on its way to the one million copies the devs were once hoping for.

For the foreseeable future, the devs aren't ready to talk about the kinds of DLC and spin-offs and follow-ups that dear old Shovel Knight enjoyed for many years, but they're not abandoning their newest baby either. "We're working on more post-release features," the devs wrote, which includes "expanded randomizer options, enemy and boss randomization, more modifiers, speedrunner features" and more ways "to do even more in Mina."

Another fan also asked the folks at Yacht Club about their unannounced 3D Shovel Knight game - Velasco previously told Bloomberg that the game was halfway done before the entire studio put all hands on deck for Mina, and pivoted back into a one-game outfit. Alec Faulkner stopped short of confirming Shovel Knight 3D, but said "most of us are currently working on a 3D game, yes!" Alright then, Alec, keep your secrets. "Not sayin more! Other than that it’s gonna be soooooooo awesome."

Co-founder Nick Wozniac went further into the state of the developer, and why splitting the team in half was probably a mistake. Here's what he had to say on the matter: "Sales are the things that keep the company afloat so it's not born from greed (mostly) that we say we'd love to see more sales, it's all about continuing to work together and make great games and reaping the rewards along the way. We are doing ok and learned a lot this cycle. I think we learned mostly that keeping the team tight and focused is what helped Mina land. Splitting the team up to work on two games was something we could have corrected a long time ago but I'm glad to be where we are now. Just gotta pocket those lessons and use them to drive you forward."

Eurogamer's five-star Mina the Hollower review called it an "adventure that takes inspiration from the greats."

#3786. A Scam Website Is Trying To Cash In On AO3 Outage By ‘Selling’ Audiobooks Of Fanfics [Update: It’s Been Taken Down]

In an attempt to prey on individuals bereft of free things to readÂ in the wake of the massive AO3 outage, a new website has seemingly popped up out of the ether, promising readers all their favorite fanfictions and the authors of said fanfics a bit of cash. The website, AO3.life (which I will not link to for reasons that will become apparent soon) purports to be the salvation of the actual AO3, the fanfiction website which was recently taken offline after a security incident and may remain down for weeks. This new website appears to have scraped a cached version of AO3, as users report older versions of their work on it, as well as works that have been deleted or made private.

The fact that this site uses AO3’s name and hosts an outdated, unauthorized version of the fanfiction website, one where works have been reposted without the authors’ consent, is bad enough. But there’s also the stank of scam permeating ao3.life. The website claims that it pays authors by selling their works as audiobooks with the proceeds split, “91% to the author, 9% to ao3.life.” All you have to do, the site claims, to either receive your cash or to remove your fics from this felonious-ass site is send them an email from the account tied to your AO3 profile.

For the love of the omegaverse, do not do this.

As many users on social media have pointed out, this is an elaborate phishing/doxxing attempt. The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the parent non-profit behind AO3, is aware of the situation and is taking steps to get the site taken down. On the AO3 subreddit, a moderator posted a message from OTW being sent to users reporting ao3.life. “We are aware and are taking action, but please be patient because the legal system is much slower than online life,” it read.

Update Tuesday November 3rd 9:22 AM: AO3.life has been taken down. Visiting the website now displays a message allegedly from the site’s administrator.

In the time this site has been up, Iâve facilitated over 2,000 takedown requests. It was never my intention to hurt so many authors – and Iâm truly sorry to you all. Thereâs no way to show my sorry better than taking this site down.

Why did I charge for AI Slop audiobooks? I doubt anyone knows how expensive it is to run a server like this, especially with the amount of usage this site got. It had 126,592 unique users within 24 hours of going up, and had terabytes of bandwidth in usage. In an attempt to keep the site up, I thought audiobooks were a good option. I sold like 11 audiobooks, if itâs any consolation.

It was never and is not my intention to hurt authors, and I hope every subequent action Iâve taken is representative of that – From an attempt at revenue sharing, to responding to takedown requests as fast as I could, to taking down the site as a whole.

The data powering this site was all from public scrapes, I have no affiliation to AO3, OTW, or anyone that breached AO3.

There was a lot of love, and a lot of hate. On Reddit and Twitter people were really mean, and there was a lot of love on other channels. Iâm grateful to everybody. I had a survey on the site for whether this site made you happy or not – It was 49% happy (3,184 yes) and 47% sad (3,057 no), which also made me realize that I wasnât doing the right thing.

Yours truly, a 17 year old from India that thought they were doing something good, Ganesh

Nightdive has unveiled the first trailer for Thief: The Tarnished Mirror, a new official expansion to Thief coming with its imminent remaster. Most exciting of all: The Tarnished Mirror is being made by the team behind The Black Parade, a 2023 mod that was one of the most exciting things to happen to the series in 20 years.

The Tarnished Mirror consists of four new missions, and is meant "as a bridge between Thief: The Dark Project and Thief 2: The Metal Age," according to an accompanying press release. Similar to The Black Parade, these new levels will leverage improvements in technology to offer more sprawling, ambitious maps than '90s PCs could handle.

The scenes from the trailer are all very Thief, but similar to The Black Parade, there's immediately more verticality than in the 1997 original game. There are also glimpses at interiors that leverage familiar Thief assets to create weirder, more surprising spaces than I'm used to from the mainline games.

The press release also indicates that The Tarnished Mirror will embrace Thief's contested legacy of horror in a similar way to The Black Parade, and that's music to my ears. I've always been a Thief undead mission defender, and The Black Parade upped the ante⁠—it's one of the scariest games I've ever played.

All told, this news about the expansion has more than made up for my disappointment at there being no PC version of the remaster's big box special edition. I may not get my tchotchke fix here, but the Thief Remaster is shaping up to be something very special.

#3784. Pokémon is teasing a massive November 30 announcement, and fans have multiple compelling theories

The Pokémon Company is up to something again. The official Pokémon website in Japan quietly launched an unconventional countdown that, if fans’ predictions are right, will expire at 9 AM EST/6 AM PT on November 30, 2026.

While the company hasn’t officially said there’s a big announcement coming at the end of November, this cheeky little stunt has already swept fans (including Serebii.net webmaster Joe Merrick) up into a maelstrom of speculation.

Ok Pokémon in Japan are counting down to something They just tweeted this with 843. On October 18th they posted this with 1025There was precisely 182 hours between the tweets. 1025-182 = 843Assuming an hourly countdown, this ends November 30th at 14:00 UTC pic.twitter.com/47y3CYhAZT

Most agree that we’re probably getting a major Pokémon Direct on November 30. November is usually an important month for the franchise, so odds are whatever’s coming on the 30th is something big. The only thing fans seem to be disagreeing on is what the Direct will be about.

The dominant theory right now is that the Direct will be entirely-or-mostly focused on Pokémon: Winds & Waves. The 10th Generation of Pokémon’s first mainline console games were officially unveiled in February with a cinematic trailer that showed off the new starter trio and the game’s Indonesian archipelago-inspired region, but we haven’t gotten any significant updates since.

Winds & Waves is set to come out sometime next year, and fans are eager to see what the games have in store. There’s plenty of reason to be excited, as a Winds & Waves-themed Direct could show us some of the region’s new Pokémon (which could include the game’s mascot Legendaries), introduce new battle mechanics, or show off how players will navigate the game’s expansive open world.

While most fans seem to agree that the November 30 announcement will be Winds & Waves-related, there’s reason to believe it could be something else. The most popular alternative theory is that we’ll get official Switch ports of Pokémon Ruby, Sapphire & Emerald.

Pokémon fans have been guessing for quite some time that a port of Ruby & Sapphire is on its way. Evidence includes a 30-second clip of Ruby & Sapphire running on an emulator posted to the official Pokémon account, and the fact that modders found Ruby, Sapphire & Emerald emulation data hidden inside Pokémon: FireRed & LeafGreen‘s Switch ports.

While the formal announcement of a Ruby, Sapphire & Emerald Switch port would be very exciting news, it’s only one of the many possibilities Pokémon fans are kicking around. Some hope the announcement will be a new Pokémon Go season, a second DLC for Poketopia, or news about the next Regulation Set for Pokémon Champions.

While it’s impossible to say exactly what The Pokémon Company has in store for us in November, it’s clear it won’t be a minor announcement. The amount of effort the Pokémon Company is putting into building up this announcement is well outside the norm for a run-of-the-mill Pokémon Direct. So whether it’s a full-onWinds & Waves feature or a mixed bag of smaller reveals, November 30, 2026, will be a big day for Pokémon fans.

One voice actor calls the AI text-to-speech tech "freeing" as "I can go and take a job somewhere else"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arc Raiders' audio director argues in favor of its AI text-to-speech, saying that "actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that."

Arc Raiders came under fire last year by using AI text-to-speech for NPC characters found throughout the game, with Embark Studios co-founder Stefan Strandberg saying "there's no end goal in replacing any actors," and that the team used it to "maximize what we can, being a small team trying to get make rich worlds right, but still staying small."

Meanwhile, the CEO of Nexon said we should "assume that every game company is now using AI." Naturally, this caused backlash from players and developers, as these minor NPC roles were ones that could have been filled by professional actors, like NPC roles in countless other games.

In an episode of Embark's "The Evolution of ARC Raiders" video series (via Eurogamer) focusing on sound and music, audio director Bence Pajor recalls previous experiences in development when teams were unable to change gameplay decisions, calling it a "true pain." Pajor explains that while the training data for the text-to-speech was made with actor's performances, he argues that it wouldn't be feasible to have them record all of the lines, saying "the actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that."

Diana Gardner who plays Celeste in the game, called the tech "freeing" as "I can go and take a job somewhere else," and if Embark needs her input, it'd be short enough that she doesn't have to cancel other gigs.

Despite arguments that using AI for performances does just that, Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg says "we are not in the industry of replacing actors," saying what the developers are doing is "the opposite." He explains, "We should celebrate the performance and give them more space. That's something I'm hoping to give to players over the coming years."

Arc Raiders devs know PvE has been "polarizing," promise to prioritize the game's "overall health and enjoyability" when deciding what to do next.

#3782. Eight years later, Elder Scrolls 6 finally has an official title, but still no release date anywhere in sight

See you soon. Or maybe not. Probably not.

As part of Bethesda’s 40th anniversary celebration, we finally have some concrete news to deliver on The Elder Scrolls.

At the end of the video below, Bethesda confirmed rumored news that the new game’s full title is The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. And this is 15 years since The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim, and over eight years since the game was originally announced at E3. Yeah, it’s been so long that E3 still existed back then.

Surely this means that the game’s development is full steam ahead now, right? I sure would hope so. Now that Starfield is behind them (and us), we can fully embrace TES6 and look forward to it soon. Or maybe not.

“Thank you for 40 years of shared memories,” Bethesda said on Twitter/X. “We can’t wait to make even more together with The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Development continues, and while it’ll be some time before we’re ready to share more, it feels great to finally reveal the name and location with you.”

Well, there you have it. I genuinely don’t know what to think or feel at the moment. Excitement? Indifference? Tiredness? I do know that I think that this game is example number one that should be given when it comes to titles being announced a bit too prematurely. Players have had expectations for years about hearing more, and so far we have two short video clips and a title confirmation in a little under a decade.

“SENTINEL is the next chapter of The Elder Scrolls,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma said. “An incredible way for Bethesda to mark 40 years of building worlds that speak to millions of players across generations. Congratulations to the team, past and present.”

It’s safe to say that this game will not be coming to Xbox Series X|S, and is destined for Project Helix or even beyond. Will it be a console-exclusive, or available on all platforms? We may find out in 2030 if we are lucky.

#3781. A former volunteer is threatening legal action against fan-made game project Skyblivion

A former volunteer is threatening legal action against Skyblivion, the long-running fan remake of Oblivion built in Skyrim's engine, over code they contributed to the project.

The unofficial project, which remakes 2006's The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion, is being made by volunteers from the TES Renewal Project, the modding group that also works on Morrowind remake Skywind.

Bethesda has allowed the project to continue on condition that it replaces all of the original game's assets, and the team continued working on it after Bethesda released its own Oblivion Remastered in April 2025.

In a statement posted to Twitter/X on 30th October, the Skyblivion team said that after the volunteer left, the two sides disagreed over the "continued use and maintenance" of their work.

A former volunteer is attempting to sue Skyblivion and we need your help pic.twitter.com/3Ee5eQTELG

The main issue was the team's decompilation of parts of that code, which it said was needed "to maintain functionality and fix issues" after its access to the original source code repository was revoked.

According to the team, the volunteer then "escalated to sending legal threats", including demands for the real names and home addresses of its volunteer team leads. The team said this was "something we couldn't accept and think is disproportionate".

The team said it has consulted legal counsel and is "completely confident in our right to maintain the code they submitted". Even so, it said it removed the code "to protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break", rebuilding that system from scratch.

Despite this, it says the threats have continued. Its post says the former volunteer is "attempting to sue", but it's not clear whether a lawsuit has actually been filed. The volunteer has not been named.

"Please don't make this a witch-hunt," the team told fans, adding that it wishes the former volunteer "the very best" and hopes to "get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with our planned release of Skyblivion".

Last December, the team delayed Skyblivion from 2025 into 2026.

#3780. GOG Explains How One Of The Most Important PC Games Ever Made Is Trapped In Licensing Hell

Westwood Studios’ Dune 2: The Building of a Dynasty isn’t the first real-time strategy game ever made, but it is one of the earliest examples of the genre and essentially provided the blueprint for what RTS games would be moving forward, inspiring Blizzard and other studios in the process. But it seems very unlikely that this important bit of PC gaming history will get an official re-release anytime soon or be part of GOG’s preservation program.Â

In a new interview with GamesRadar, Marcin Paczynski, senior business development and partnerships manager at PC gaming store GOG, explained just how complicated and messy the rights are to 1992’s Dune 2. And it comes down to the influential RTS being based on a movie based on a book, from a studio owned by another company; in this case, EA.

“So currently, Electronic Arts has the game code, the assets, all of the rights to those things, and all the materials around the game,” explained Paczynski.

“But of course, they do not own the [Dune] IP. The problem with the IP is that it is not directly owned by [Dune writer Frank Herbert’s estate], because the games were not based on the books; they were actually based on the movie from 1984. That movie was created by Universal Pictures, and the main producer for that movie was [Dino De Laurentiis]. The problem is that he also has part of that movie license with him. But he died 15 years ago.”

That means De Laurentiis’ estate owns a “portion” of Dune 2. And then there’s another complication. Legendary Pictures owns the IP rights for the new Dune movies and has a deal with Funcom to create Dune Awakening, a survival gameÂ set in the Dune universe. And according to Paczynski, there’s some amount of “exclusivity” included in that deal.

Exactly how or even if that deal would get in the way of re-releasing Westwood’s classic Dune games, including Dune 2000, is “currently not clear,” says Paczynski. But it’s yet one more issue to deal with if anyone were to try to bring back these important classics.

For Paczynski, this is likely a frustrating situation as he considers Dune 2 as one of his personal “holy grails” for GOG to bring back and preserve.

“It’s on the top of my list, my personal one, because this is a game that I have a lot of nostalgia for,” said Paczynski. “The situation is a good example of how bad it can get with the licensing situation of a game.”

It’s also a great example of why fan projects tend to be the betterâand often onlyâoption for playing classic games decades after launch. Fans making patches and mods don’t (generally) have to deal with lawyers and legal hurdles in the same way GOG and other companies have to when trying to bring back a classic.

Still, I hope one day Dune 2 is given a proper, officially supported re-release on modern PC storefronts so it can be easily played by new gamers. Dune essentially ushered in what would become the modern RTS and, as a result, led to the creation of games like Warcraft, which then led to MOBAs like League of Legends. It’s an important piece of gaming history that deserves a return.

#3779. Silent Hill: Townfall adds new Hard difficulty in latest update

Silent Hill: Townfall has added a new Hard difficulty mode and rebalanced every existing setting to make room for it.

The update, patch 1.6.0, went live on PS5, Steam, and the Epic Games Store earlier this week, according to patch notes published by Konami. Konami said the rebalance is designed to create "a smoother difficulty curve for players to choose from".

As part of that rebalance, resources have been adjusted in some sections of the game, and enemies' hearing now gets sharper as the difficulty level goes up. Your position is now visible on the map in whichever mode you pick, while the reduction to the main enemy's attack severity now applies only in Story Mode.

Anyone who picks Nightmare for their first playthrough will now see a warning screen. The difficulty selection menu also gives a clearer summary of how the options differ.

SILENT HILL: TownfallNotice: Game Update (Patch 1.6.0)An update tuning gameplay and addressing some in-game issues is now available.Please check that the version number in the lower right corner of the main menu is displayed as v1.6.155963.*The PlayStation®5 version is…

The update also improves the valve status lighting for colourblind players, adds more hints and tutorials, and tweaks the wording of some puzzle hints and items. The options menu has been reorganised into clearer categories, and the controls remapping option has been renamed to make it clear that keyboard and mouse commands can be remapped there too, not just controllers.

PC players also get a new DLSS Ray Reconstruction option, alongside the usual general improvements and bug fixes.

To check you're on the latest version, look for v1.6.155963 in the lower right corner of the main menu on PC, or v1.6.156035 on PS5.

Developed by Screen Burn and published by Konami, Silent Hill: Townfall launched on PS5 and PC on 24th September. Matt said Townfall showed Silent Hill's "stellar revival continues as new developer Screen Burn melds stealth, meticulous world design, and a dash of social realism for a different sort of survival horror", and awarded it four out of five stars in Eurogamer's Silent Hill: Townfall review.
