#3714. GTA 6 Pre-Load Times, Install Size, And Global Release Times Confirmed

Grand Theft Auto 6Grand Theft Auto VIGTA 6Pre-Load

We’re just over two weeks out from the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 and Rockstar Games has finally revealed all of the details people need to know about getting the digital-only open-world game installed on their gaming console of choice.

The studio also confirmed that, yes, GTA 6 has a whopping 212GB install size, so start making room for that and god help you if you have an Xbox Series S. Here’s everything you need to know about getting GTA 6 ready to play for its release on November 19, 2026.

Digital pre-loading on PlayStation 5 will start globally on Tuesday, November 10 at midnight local time. On Xbox Series X|S, pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12 a.m. GMT, which is 7:00 p.m. ET on the previous day, November 9.

If you pre-order GTA 6 digitally, you’ll have access to pre-load the game immediately. If you are waiting for one of the codes in a box to ship to your home or be picked up in store, those will become available starting November 12. You’ll be able to take that code, redeem it, and immediately start pre-loading the game.

That’s a big file size, and console servers are going to get hammered when everyone starts trying to download it at once. To put it in perspective, 212GB is roughly one third of the available storage on a base PS5 and roughly a quarter of the available storage on a 1TB model. On Xbox Series S, it’s closer to half. In addition to taking some time depending on the speed of your internet, you’ll want to make sure you have your library cleared of any non-essential games. Good luck to you if you have children who are constantly swapping between a dozen different games every day.

The global release times for when GTA 6 goes live were previously announced, and unfortunately the U.S. is one of the last time zones to get access to the game.

Yes, the game will have been out in some parts of the world for roughly 18 hours by the time GTA 6 goes live stateside. My advice is to just stay logged out that day.

The Marvel Cinematic Universe is constantly growing, thanks to exciting new projects arriving in theaters and streaming with a Disney+ subscription. Fans have a number of upcoming Marvel movies to look forward to, but the hype around Avengers: Doomsday is at a fever pitch. Folks are looking for any clues about what The Russo Brothers have up their sleeve, and there's a new reasons why fans (including me) think that Tom Holland's Spider-Man might end up having a surprise appearance.

What we know about Avengers: Doomsday is very limited, which is why moviegoers have been filling in the blanks with rumors and theories. The Doomsday cast list is a huge one, but Kevin Feige confirmed that more surprise appearances will be included as well. Merch for the movie has been rolling out, including a collaboration with Ray-Ban inspired by a number of heroes. Namely Captain America, Doctor Doom, Deadpool and (you guessed it) Spider-Man.

Some fans thought this might indicate that Deadpool is in Doomsday, and the concept of Spider-Man popping up seems even more likely. After all, Brand New Day and the next Avengers movie filmed at the time in Pinewood Studios in England. So it wouldn't take much more than some clever scheduling for Tom Holland to run over to the other end of the studio and shoot some footage as Peter Parker. Plus, he's one of the most popular characters in the entire shared universe.

The credits scene from Spider-Man: Brand New Day seemed to tease the web slinger popping up in either Doomsday or its sequel Secret Wars. Specifically the latter, as it showed a Spider-Man being spotted in space. Still, the Spidey Ray-Bans have other moviegoers crossing their fingers that Tom Holland's beloved hero will get to join the forthcoming battle again Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day became the highest grossing movie of all time upon its release, so it's clear that folks are invested in Tom Holland's ongoing tenure as the web swinger. As such, it seems like a no-brainer that The Russos and Marvel would want him included in the shared universe's next big crossover moments. We'll just have to see whether or not this theory ends up coming to fruition.

Deadpool & Wolverine also broke records at the box office, so it's possible that Ray-Ban was simply releasing new Marvel merch based on its most popular characters. Although since Deadpool and Spider-Man haven't been officially confirmed for Doomsday yet, the new sunglasses have set the internet ablaze. Clearly the Marvel fandom is invested in the next Avengers movie, and it should be fascinating to see which characters actually appear.

All will be revealed when Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Fingers crossed we see Spider-Man pop up throughout it mysterious runtime.

#3712. The Borderlands series has sold over 100 million copies, and Gearbox is "cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year"

The Borderlands series has sold more than 100m copies across all games, developer Gearbox Software has announced. No surprise, then - the studio also said it's cooking up "big plans" for the evergreen looter shooter's future.

"The Borderlands franchise has officially crossed 100 million units sold," Gearbox boasted in a blog post published today. "There aren't many franchises that have ever hit that milestone, and we certainly didn't get here on our own. For us, it started with that first Borderlands in 2009, and we've been excited about everyone who has joined us in the Borderlands along the way. Borderlands has always had an incredibly passionate community. We've been through a lot together, and your feedback pushes us to make even greater games."

So, where can Vault Hunters expect to go next? Gearbox just finished up on Borderlands 4's Year One roadmap - which included two new playable characters, two Story Packs and more - and it's now "cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year." There's no concrete information about what that looks like for now, but the studio promised Weekly Activity refreshes and Community Challenges will chug on in the meantime.

"We're also taking a bigger look at the franchise as a whole. Where can we take it next? What characters do you want to spend more time with? What stories deserve a payoff? A huge part of that is listening to you," the studio wrote. "All that said, big plans take time, and we need some room to work. You can trust that we'll talk more when the time is right. Now is your chance to influence what we'll say."

Borderlands 4 itself experienced a "softer" than expected launch, thanks partly to the game's wonky PC performance, though it seems to have been a success in the long run. A promised Switch 2 port was also indefinitely delayed earlier in the year. We haven't heard much about that handheld version since, but Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick did say the team were focusing on getting Borderlands 4 into tip-top shape before trying to bring it elsewhere.

In Eurogamer's Borderlands 4 review, Rick Lane said the shooter bought a "more sensible script and a true open world to its pseudo-cel-shaded gun-show, but these moderate improvements are undermined by frustrating exploration and combat that takes too long to properly shine."

#3711. 10 Hacks Ever Siri AI User Should Know

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

If you're like me, you've spent years ignoring most of Siri's functionality. Sure, it's great for setting timers, making calls, and sending a text. But that's kind of it—Apple's promise of an "always-on" digital assistant never truly delivered.

But that's finally changed with the recent launch of Siri AI. Fifteen years after debuting the app on the iPhone 4S and four years after the release of ChatGPT, Apple has taken the time to build out its own private Apple Foundation Models (with little help from Google) that work both on-device and on Apple's servers to give quick responses to your queries. Siri AI's answers are short, to the point, and actually useful. However, the conversational side isn't the only new thing about Siri AI. In fact, once you scratch the surface, you'll find Siri AI features embedded across the entire iOS and macOS ecosystem. Here's how to get the most out of Apple's new, enhanced digital assistant.

Siri AI is already tuned for brevity. Compared to Gemini or Claude, its responses are short and to the point. But still, if you ask something with your voice, it responds using voice as well. I personally prefer to quickly read through Siri responses. If you’re like me, you can enable a hidden setting that makes sure that Siri always answers silently, no matter if you’re writing to it or using your voice. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and switch to the Silent Response option.

On the other hand, if you prefer to listen to Siri's responses, it's worth it to spend some time fine-tuning them. If you have an iPhone that’s under two years old, you have access to a more expressive Siri voice. Siri AI has an Expressive Voice feature that works on iPhone 17 Pro and higher, iPhone Air, and Macs with an M3 processor or higher (at least 12GB RAM).

To find this feature, go to Settings > Siri > Voice. Here, you can change the Pace to make Siri faster or slower. The big feature is the Expressivity slider; you can use it to make Siri sound brighter and more enthusiastic, rather than flat. You also have several voice options at the top (color-coded).

Visual Intelligence is deeply integrated into iOS 27 and macOS 27, and it turns anything on your screen into a source that Siri AI can act upon. It can search anything on your screen, and even take action on things it finds out. You can highlight any text on an iPhone, tap and hold, and choose the Ask Siri option. On the Mac, Ask Siri is the first option in the right-click menu. Choose a file, select text, and get started talking to Siri.

But it goes further. Just pull up Siri AI on your iPhone or Mac and start asking questions about what you’re seeing on screen. If you’re seeing a photo of a cafe on Instagram, ask where it is, or ask Siri to open it in Maps. If you’re watching a scene from a movie or a TV show, ask Siri where it’s from.

Clean Up was part of Apple Intelligence features in iOS 18, but it wasn’t great. It used on-device models to remove objects, and the results were lacking. Now that Apple runs its own Apple Foundation Models in Private Cloud Compute, it can securely process images on its servers, and the Clean Up process is much better. It now removes objects from photos very reliably, and even accounts for shadows. But to use this, you have to make sure to use the High Quality feature (instead of the default Auto mode).

Tap the Edit button in a photo, go to Tools > Clean Up, and from the top, switch to the High Quality option. Now brush over or tap an object you want to remove. Then, tap Clean Up and wait for a while until Apple’s servers complete the process. Tap Done to save the changes.

One of the most tedious parts of using the Calendar app is manually entering multiple events from a complicated schedule—say, for a season's worth of your kid’s soccer practices, or your college course's weekly lecture schedule. With Visual Intelligence in iOS 27, this is now table stakes: You can point your iPhone camera towards a schedule or take a screenshot of one, then tap the Add to Calendar button. Siri will recognize all the events, and you’ll get an option to add them to the calendar individually or all at once.

Siri AI's Mail integration is a hidden gem. Once your iPhone or Mac is done indexing your local data from Mail, you can use Siri AI to triage and manage your Mail without even opening the Mail app. In my testing, it works really well, especially because Siri AI understands the context of an email. This means you don't need to remember the exact details about the sender or the subject. You can just ask something like, "Find all emails about my flights from last week and send them to my accountant." You can also ask it to do things for you. For example, you can say, "Archive all the emails from Walmart from last month," and it will give you a one-button option to do just that.

When you start using the new Siri AI more often, you'll realize that it asks for confirmation way too often. For things like deleting mail, that's useful. But for sending messages, less so. There is a hidden setting that removes the extra step when it comes to sending messages via Siri. Go to Settings > Siri > Responses and enable Automatically Send Messages.

After the Siri AI upgrade in iOS 27, I find myself using the Camera Control often, and you should try it too. Just press and hold the Camera Control button to launch the camera's Siri mode. Point towards anything you want to find out more about and tap the big Siri icon. In a second or two, you will get the Siri response at the top, along with relevant actions based on what you're looking at. This feature is genuinely useful, and if you don't like using the Camera Control (or don't have access to it on your iPhone), you can also add the Siri AI shortcut to the lock screen, Control Center, or the Action button.

While Shortcuts has been one of Apple's most powerful features, it's also one of the hardest to use. Making an automation requires setting up steps, selecting variables, and thinking about chronology, and more. With Siri AI, Apple is trying to reduce that burden. And when it comes to simpler stuff that an everyday iPhone user needs, it works.

For example, you can open Shortcuts, create a new shortcut, and use the Describe a shortcut feature to talk about a Shortcut you want to build in natural language. You can ask Siri to create a daily morning Shortcut that shows you the day's weather, upcoming calendar events, and the to-do list for the day. You can also ask it to create a Shortcut that converts images in batches and creates new notes with a pre-made template.

While Apple is now using its own Apple Foundation Models for the new Siri AI, ChatGPT isn’t technically gone. If you have a complex question, or if Siri AI’s answer isn’t doing the trick, you can still summon ChatGPT from the Siri AI app (no need to go to the ChatGPT app for this). Tap on the text field in the Siri app, choose the Ask option and then switch to the ChatGPT service. Siri AI is quite intelligent at routing, so if ChatGPT can’t answer, it will route you back to Siri AI’s own models.

#3710. Yakuza creator's new studio and its debut game Gang of Dragon are no more after losing funding from NetEase

Nagoshi Studio has officially shut down and its first game called Gang of Dragon is seemingly no more, months after publisher NetEase pulled funding from the Yakuza-like project.

Toshihiro Nagoshi (often cited as the creator of the brilliant Yakuza and Like A Dragon game series) opened his new studio in 2021 and announced his next game with a very familiar title almost one year ago. Now, the Tokyo-based developer has closed its doors, as confirmed in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

The news comes months after employees were told that the studio's future was at risk due to NetEase's funding cuts. Nagoshi Studio reportedly needed another £33.1 million (about $44.4m at the time) to get Gang of Dragon past the finish line - a paycheck NetEase purportedly didn't want to cough up.

The China-based Marvel Rivals and Where Winds Meet publisher has been significantly scaling back on international investments these past few years. Visions of Mana developer Ouka Studios was shut down just after launching its gorgeous action game, Worlds Untold (a studio formed by Mass Effect veteran Mac Walters) had to pause operations to find a new partner, and Halo Infinite lead Jerry Hook's studio also ran into very similar issues last year.

Some developers have been a little luckier. Suda51's Grasshopper Manufacture saved itself with a management buyout and now operates as an independent developer, for one.

Not much is known about Gang of Dragon, but its debut trailer featured the violent crime and high drama you'd expect from Nagoshi's previous work. The game also starred Ma Dong-seok, the acclaimed actor you might recognise from films such as Train to Busan and Marvel's Eternals.

PC Gamer's annual list of the 100 best PC games you can play—updated for 2026

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Welcome to the PC Gamer Top 100—our annual list of the best games you can play right now. Every year, we look at the hundreds of thousands of PC games that are available to buy, and think, "yes, we can whittle this down into a numbered list". Hubris? Yes. A months-long crucible of heated arguments and impassioned pleas? Also yes.

More than anything, the Top 100 is designed to capture a moment in time. It's a place where the 'canon' classics of the past rub shoulders against the fresh new hotness. Where being a game that a significant portion of the team currently loves is as important as being a game that is recognised worldwide for its contributions to the medium.

It is a deeply subjective process—a way for PC Gamer's editorial team to advocate for the games they're passionate about. One member of our team has spent years attempting to get Overwatch back on the list, taking every opportunity to persuade their fellow editors to give it a chance. Not every entry required that level of dedication to earn its spot, but every pick is a game that at least a handful of our staff cares deeply about.

Ahead of the vote, the PC Gamer team is free to nominate any PC game for voting, giving us a longlist of over 300 games. Each member of the team is then asked to rate those games subjectively across three weighted categories:

The weightings are designed around the Top 100's function as an annual, ever-changing list. Too much weight to Importance, and the list stagnates. Too much to Freshness, and there's no consistency year-to-year. Quality is the most important category because, ultimately, if we don't think a game is actually very good, it doesn't make the list.

The sum of each game's ratings is divided by its number of voters, and then run through a few special formulae—including a penalty for games that receive too few votes—to produce the final Top 100 Score for each game.

We then make some manual adjustments. In the interest of variety we mostly restrict the list to one game per series—only including multiple if we think the games are different enough from each other to be worth mentioning, as with Baldur's Gate 2 and Baldur's Gate 3. Otherwise, the lower scoring game in a series is removed. We also let editors pitch for a change to the list—each of which is voted on by the wider team, and only ratified if it gets majority approval.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

What's left is the 100 games you find below. Some might claim it folly—attempting to wrestle the varied tastes of our editorial team into a list of games we wholeheartedly recommend. Nevertheless, we're sure that within these entries, you'll find something new to love.

Elie Gould: I'm in no way a MOBA-lover but I sure do love Deadlock. I love its fantastically written characters, exciting and experimental game design, and its mode for dummies: Street Brawl.

Jacob Ridley: Welp, Elie has called me out. I play Deadlock for dummies, otherwise known as Street Brawl, and it's something special. A large cast of otherworldly characters keeps every round fresh. It's surprisingly accessible through excellent character, UI, and game design—a high skill ceiling, but fun all the way down. Great game, and I'm yet to even try the MOBA mode.

Elie Gould: That wasn't a call out, Jacob. I also love and play Deadlock for dummies, it rocks!

Andrea Shearon: It's me, the MOBA-lover logging in to say I've only put a handful of hours into Deadlock and already love it. I'm the reverse of Elie and not into hero shooters, but Deadlock (and Calico) have won me over.

Harvey Randall: It's also me, the person on the PC Gamer team with 360+ hours in this thing—and while I do (unfortunately, it's a character flaw) know how to play MOBAs, Deadlock is shaping up to be the best-in-class of the entire genre. Which means, as my fellows have stated, it also has an absolute ton going for it outside of just being a very good example of itself.

Valve has cooked up one of its coolest settings—a supernatural 1950s New York where barrel mimics lurk on street corners and Lovecraftian gods play at their own versions of the Grand Budapest. And while it's not yet finished, the fact it's getting record-high concurrents should tell you just how much Valve has cooked here.

Jake Tucker: I've tried and failed to get into Deadlock a few times now, and the main draw is the incredible world. MOBAs could be accused, usually, of being a little bit of a fantasy hodgepodge, but Deadlock's setting is consistent and fascinating, a tiny city for you to explore each game.

Released: March 19, 2026 | Top 100 Score: 215.31

Morgan Park: I consider Death Stranding 2 the perfect kind of sequel. It builds on all of the fantastic hiking, delivery, and construction stuff that ruled about the original while rethinking what kinda sucked (combat). The addition of proper bandit camps and expanded combat options really rounds out its sandbox into something special—a contemplative walking simulator, a complex logistics game, and a memorable immersive sim. The first Death Stranding is one of my favorites, but On The Beach upstages it on all fronts. Personally, it should rate higher.

Sean Martin: Death Stranding 2 has a similar magic to Control, but where that game juxtaposes the mundanity of office life with paranormal occurrences, Death Stranding 2 actually makes logistics work ridiculously fun. I built a little truck, slapped as many batteries to the outside as I could, and drove it across Australia, even through Timefall events, which is more than any delivery man should have to deal with.

Jody Macgregor: I'm the guy who thinks the first one was better. The deliveries were more challenging, and the setting more mysterious. I loved not knowing what was going on and then slowly getting to grips with this bizarro whale-themed apocalypse. By comparison Death Stranding 2 has a bad case of the exposition dumps, with Dollman in particular basically existing just to parp out explanations in case you didn't understand the thing that literally just happened.

Fraser Brown: I loved the first one, but I refuse to spend £70 on a PC game. I have a dog to feed.

Released: February 17, 2022 | Top 100 Score: 216.90

Sean Martin: What we talk about when we talk about Total War: Warhammer 3 is really Immortal Empires, the colossal campaign culmination of a decade-long trilogy of games and expansions. I've played Total War almost my entire life, but Immortal Empires stands at the pinnacle of campaign gameplay—a fantastical brewing pot of fun factions and units, enough to enthral any would-be Warhammer-lover.

And it keeps growing and mutating like some endlessly ravenous troll. The Lords of the End Times expansion arrived recently and introduced the iconic period alongside a fresh endgame rework.

Jody Macgregor: One of those Lords of the End Times, the Great Necromancer Nagash, has a nailbiting campaign where basically everyone hates you and your economy is mid, but fortunately you are a gigantic bony badass (seriously, even his bootlaces look skeletal) who cannot be stopped. Your minions are constantly failing and you have to go bail them out personally, arriving like Darth Vader on the day an officer screwed up big time, then absolutely demolishing whatever opposition was causing the trouble. It's glorious.

Fraser Brown: I used to be a diehard historical Total War boy, but the work Creative Assembly has done on Warhammer has been too damn impressive. There were some bumps in the road, but the most recent string of DLCs have been incredible, culminating in one of my favourite expansions. God, Nagash is good. OK, he's actually incredibly evil. But I love this lich.

Jake Tucker: Hard same, why would I ever want to play as medieval knights smashing each other when I could play as Skaven fighting against monstrous ogres?

Released: March 10, 2015 | Top 100 Score: 218.90

Fraser Brown: Still the best urban city builder around, even after all these years. The sequel is better than it was at launch, but the OG is still comfy on its city planner throne. City planners do get thrones, right? They should.

Phil Savage: There's no shortage of options if you want a focused city builder that hones in on a particular vibe or scenario. But if you want pure, maximalist city-building—the full uncut hit of zone distribution, traffic management and tourism expansion—Cities: Skylines is still the only true game in town.

Released: March 20, 2020 | Top 100 Score: 219.27

Morgan Park: The list of big-budget singleplayer shooters is depressingly small these days, but even if they were the hotness, I don't think Doom Eternal would have trouble keeping its FPS throne. Eternal is the ultimate marriage of acrobatics and heft, casting the Slayer as a helldiving fighter jet with dashes, jumps, but no wallrun. Though sometimes dinged for some brave difficulty spikes, this is still peak modern Doom, and a true PC shooter—as in, you really should play it with a mouse and keyboard.

Shaun Prescott: I've struggled to care much about new FPS games since Doom Eternal. It's so unrelenting, so exhausting, that I think it filled my cup forever.

Released: August 8, 2006 (Alpha) | Top 100 Score: 219.30

Lincoln Carpenter: Dwarf Fortress is one of the most distilled forms of PC gaming. Acclimating to its demands and expectations is almost a lifestyle in itself, but you're rewarded for the effort with a sprawling fantasy management sim and a deeply simulated roguelike, with systems for modeling nerve damage and geographic water drainage and civilizational ruin. It's a synthesis of conscious craft and procedural generation, an engine for a long tradition of oral storytelling, and the product of the years-long and ongoing effort of obsessive software wizards. It's an absurd achievement of fantasy simulation, and its creators only intend on doubling down.

Oh, and it regularly produces patch notes like "Made the corpses of small animals that die out of water stop teleporting"—the surest sign of quality one could ask for.

Joshua Wolens: I'm genuinely convinced Dwarf Fortress might be the best game ever made. At the very least, if I were given some sort of ambassadorial role where I had to explain the power of videogames to an alien race, DF would be the first thing I showed them.

Released: July 7, 2016 | Top 100 Score: 220.67

Lauren Morton: Inside is one of those bucket list puzzle games you play once and remember fondly forever. I wish I could bottle those "Oh do they want me to… Oh wow, of course," moments that you can only ever experience once in a game and only one game in a decade truly gives you. This is that game, a surreal and creepy descent into sci-fi horror that so many sidescroll puzzlers with children in imminent danger have tried to capture since. It's nigh on perfect level design: beauty and blood pressure-spiking combined.

Andy Chalk: Inside is so good. I had no idea what was going on at any given moment or what the hell it was all about when it was over, but the vibe was pure and immaculate: Horrifying yet starkly beautiful, showing just enough of its world to satisfy without surrendering the mystery, and having the balls to end inconclusively—and, frankly, incomprehensibly. Importantly, too, Inside doesn't overstay its welcome. It's a short, sharp, surreal shock that'll leave you too wondering what the hell it was all about when it's all over.

Sean Martin: If we're talking space occupied in my brain relative to hour count, Inside is one of the most memorable, atmospheric, and smart side-scrollers I've ever played.

Released: April 24, 2018 | Top 100 Score: 221.14

Evan Lahti: Mechs are metal piñatas. Their modular durability make them the most fun-to-shoot targets in video games, more than Nazi zombies, helicopters, or terrorists. Mechs die gradually: first layers of armor, then internal structure (a mech's bones, basically), then a weapon or other component. Worst-case, an ammo compartment explodes, annihilating the equipment around it. That combat pacing is a perfect template for a video game, and it works even better in the context of an XCOM-style campaign where you're a mercenary company that's scavenging parts over time and making risk-reward judgments on which contracts to accept.

Lincoln Carpenter: The real magic trick of BattleTech is Harebrained Schemes' ability to make speed and motion so crucial in a turn-based tactics game about massive, hulking war machines. A slow mech is just an easy target.

Fraser Brown: One of the worst things Paradox ever did was not let Harebrained Schemes work on another BattleTech game. The good news is that this one has so many great mods that you can make your own sequel.

Jake Tucker: One of the best turn-based strategy games ever made, the fact this didn't spawn a multi-part series or even get the level of support of several of Paradox's other titles makes me sad. There's something about the fantasy of running an intergalactic band of mechanised mercenaries that nothing else quite hits and has got me installing this game again on my second screen while writing this entry.

Released: September 4, 2025 | Top 100 Score: 221.14

Sean Martin: Year after year, I've advocated for Hollow Knight's position on this list, but I'm more than happy to see Silksong succeed. Scaling the kingdom of Pharloom, from its abyss-shrouded depths to its towering silken spires, is a frustrating endeavour, but I'll be damned if it's not the richest action-platforming experience you'll ever have. Hollow Knight punches above its weight constantly and Silksong is no different, weaving together masterful combat, exploration, and platforming, with an infamous ability to make you delight and despair in equal measure.

Harvey Randall: Despair really is the name of the game, here—while I like Silksong for all the normal reasons (its gorgeous setting, its excellent combat, its beautiful music), part of what enraptured me about it was its animosity towards the player. Silksong is a jerk to you. Hidden benches, traps, unreasonable runbacks, poison maggot swamps and infuriating side-quests. But that acts as a counterbalance to its beauty, and gives it enough personality that I just kept coming back to it.

Released: March 5, 2026 | Top 100 Score: 221.33

Rory Norris: Time and time again, Bungie has proven it's the best in the business when it comes to the simple joy of shooting virtual guns. Marathon combines impeccable weapon feel and a deep toybox with the innate tension of an extraction shooter for truly nail-biting action. Add to that its knack for environmental and mechanics design honed with Destiny's endgame, and you've got the most intricate, cerebral, unchained extraction shooter for those sickos willing to learn its ways.

Phil Savage: Arc Raiders is definitely the better game, but damn does Marathon's PvP feel good.

Issy van der Velde: Improving is an incredibly rewarding feeling. At launch I was a scared little runner, now I'm an Arachne angel of death

Jacob Ridley: My obsessive interest in this game during its first two weeks then sudden, complete drop-off to not playing it again since—not even once—should be studied by scientists.

Released: September 30, 2025 | Top 100 Score: 221.40

Evan Lahti: "If by our deaths a single drop of noble blood should water the earth, they shall not be in vain." Compared to the 1998 original on PlayStation, Tactics' contemporary English translation is extraordinarily Shakespearean. This is Japanese, turn-based King Lear. Soft colors and art direction blend cuteness with a backstabbing medieval tale.

There are charming, dated aspects to this chesslike RPG, like the need to grind random combats to level up critical abilities like Auto-Potion, but the depth of the jobs system and a light sandbox campaign structure makes Tactics enduring. You've also gotta love the outright strangeness of some of the job classes: the Orator (there's an actual "Lecture an enemy to sleep" ability), the Calculator (target spells based on prime numbers), stealing weapons or armor outright off of enemies as a Thief—all of which resist modern notions of a damage-maxing meta in favor of playing Tactics with a touch of silliness.

Released: October 30, 2025 | Top 100 Score: 221.59

Rory Norris: While Tarkov might be more gnarly and Marathon more satisfying shooting, Arc Raiders is wholly unique in how it has naturally, seemingly accidentally, become a social sim. Blasting players and machines is sublime, but making friends with strangers on the surface and the chaos that ensues are among my fondest moments in any game.

Evan Lahti: Can't understate the technical achievement of the ARCs themselves from an animation and pathfinding perspective. These are the best, most dynamic and unpredictable robot enemies to ever grace a video game. Even the lowly Tick has a small chance of screwing a seasoned player in the right circumstances.

Sean Martin: For me it's the Fireflies, they're such genuine buggers, always setting me aflame at the worst possible moment. But honestly, I wouldn't change them. The wild variety of ARC machines and how they insidiously permeate each map is part of what's kept me coming back even a year later. With the Frozen Trail's addition of raid-style activities like the Fallen Emperor and Arc Frigate, I'm excited for the game's current trajectory.

Released: October 6, 2014 | Top 100 Score: 221.60

Sean Martin: Peak cinema is the only way to describe Alien: Isolation. It's undeniable that the Xenomorph's elaborate AI, which stalks you through Sevastopol space station, redefined the survival-horror genre. But for me, its greater success lies in creating a game that feels exactly like its movie counterpart. We see all sorts of films made from old games, but few games made from old films, and almost none that achieve such aesthetic parity with their source material—it's a monumental achievement, and another reason to get excited for the sequel.

Issy van der Velde: 12 years later and I still scream every time the Xenomorph drops down from a vent right in front of me.

Fraser Brown: It took me a decade to finish Alien: Isolation because it simply scared the absolute shit out of me. Playing for an hour left me a sweaty, cowardly mess. Incredible game.

Joshua Wolens: They should never have given you the flamethrower. By the game's end I was using it to shoo away the xenomorph like spraying a water bottle at a stray cat.

Released: May 16, 2011 | Top 100 Score: 221.70

Andrea Shearon: I often joke I'll love any game handing me a set of Legos, but Terraria is a particularly good set. I've been digging holes to hell and hacking up mutant eyeballs for well over a decade now, and I'm still not tired of it. While all of my friends were playing Minecraft, I was in my own little survival sandbox corner with Terraria. The 2D side-scroller was always more my style, and after this year's update, I'm back to regularly building NPC castles and spelunking for treasures.

Jake Tucker: I've been playing Terraria for what feels like my entire adult life, and I still find things that make me squeal with delight. The developers have a fantastic sense of what would be fun in their own game. Each and every update, including this year's surprisingly huge content pack, feels essential.

Released: August 10, 2023 | Top 100 Score: 222.00

Elie Gould: I've been gunning for Overwatch to get onto the Top 100 ever since I rocked up at PC Gamer and seeing it finally do so after a monumental 10th year is pretty special. An absolute staple of the genre, Team 4 has managed to turn the ship around with great effort from a stagnating hero shooter to an FPS game that's experimental, polished, and continues to be a hell of a lot of fun.

Rory Norris: Don't forget the monkey scientist and hamster in a wrecking ball.

Harvey Randall: I admit it—after a long time of Elie trying to get me to play Overwatch (there definitely has not been a gun to my head at any point, and I'm not saying this because there currently is one) I've got to give fair dues: Overwatch is pretty fun at the moment. It's a very competent hero shooter, and the foibles of Overwatch 2, which put me off the game in the first place, have mostly been done away with.

Released: May 13, 2020 | Top 100 Score: 222.00

Rory Norris: Deep Rock Galactic is a rare co-op game that actually demands you work together to creatively solve problems. Each class brings unique tools to help you survive the bug-infested caves of Hoxxes IV, from a zipline to drills. That's not to mention their banter, which plays into DRG's cynical, blue collar humour.

Mix these Dwarves into a cocktail of unique, challenging enemy design, procedural level generation, and some of the most creative weapons I've seen, and it's easily the most fun I've had with the genre. Rock and stone, to the bone.

Lincoln Carpenter: Deep Rock's gameplay just has such a pleasant rhythm: Punch your way into the next procedural cave, light it up to see what you're working with, figure out how to navigate up to that delicious Morkite seam glittering above you, fight guns blazing with your backs against the wall when a swarm catches your scent, repeat. It's an enduring delight.

Released: May 5, 2022 | Top 100 Score: 221.17

Issy van der Velde: Like all great sci-fi, Citizen Sleeper uses its futuristic setting to explore a very current problem. Trapped on derelict space station the Eye and caught between a corrupt trade union, gang, and your former corporate owners, you play as a Sleeper whose mind has been digitised and put into a decaying robot body. The expensive stabilizer needed to keep from falling apart can easily be swapped for numerous real-world analogs: insulin, inhalers, hormones, antidepressants, even food and water. The fact that the need for stabilizer is the result of planned obsolescence only makes the game's parallels to our present day even more conspicuous.

I managed to carve out a nice life on the Eye despite the horrors of capitalism, and maybe that's the point—you may not change the whole world, but you can change yours.

Harvey Randall: Citizen Sleeper is one of those games that caught me at a very important time in my life—new job, new city, and big, scary changes. In the same way that I found a home in real life, I found one on Erlin's Eye: An apartment, a cat I said hello to, friends and responsibilities pushing through the industrial megastructure like green shoots.

It's also just a remarkably clever game—that journey being reflected in its mechanics, too. It slowly fades from a harsh resource management game into something more like a visual novel, and that's far from an accident.

Released: October 17, 2005 | Top 100 Score: 223.09

Jake Tucker: Some shooters turn firefights from a shooting gallery into a puzzle. Those shooters are not FEAR, a shooter that turns every firefight into the coolest action sequence of all time. Shotguns blow your enemies in half, the nailgun pins them to walls and grenades turn rooms into the lobby scene from The Matrix. Behind the scenes, incredible AI and some great encounter design keep you moving forwards, but FEAR is the greatest fire-and-forget FPS there is, where the rule of cool is in charge.

Andy Chalk: FEAR was scary as hell when it was new, and that part of it has faded but it's still a powerful FPS nut-punch that'll suck the wind right out of you. Tight, looping level design, AI that'll mess you up, and some of the best videogame guns ever made deliver unsurpassed close quarters combat: The shotgun and Penetrator get all the love but for my money the hard staccato of the G2A2 assault rifle is where it's at—and now I want to replay FEAR again.

Joshua Wolens: One of the illustrious—and sadly few—games that let you pin your enemies to the wall, and the best of them.

Released: November 20, 2009 | Top 100 Score: 223.11

Elie Gould: Left 4 Dead 2 is still a hell of a lot of fun. Perhaps it's nostalgia but I don't think any other zombie game has nailed the gruesome pleasure of killing off the undead quite like this gem. You'll still find me dragging my friends into Diescraper Redux despite being thrown from the top more times than I'd care to admit.

Phil Savage: This is a surprise inclusion for me. Left 4 Dead 2 is fine, but I'd argue Fatshark has eclipsed its brand of four-player co-op. I'd take Vermintide 2 or Darktide every time.

Harvey Randall: I've got to disagree with Phil a little bit, here—while I would personally rather play Darktide or Vermintide 2 as someone who likes a little meta-progression, there is absolutely something refreshing about the simplicity of Left 4 Dead 2. No classes, no gear, no fumbling about with equipment or meta-progression or cosmetics. You hop in and you shoot a zombie with your shotgun and that's that.

Released: September 17, 2023 | Top 100 Score: 225.00

Phil Savage: Yes, yes, GTA 6 is right around the corner—for consoles, at least. For now, though, GTA 5 is still well worth your attention on PC. The base game is great, but it's found life beyond that through Rockstar's own (admittedly janky, but incredibly expansive) GTA Online, as well as the extensive modding scene that encompasses everything from quick jokes to full, in-depth roleplaying server support. To this day, there's little else that rivals the chaos of GTA Online's heist missions—they're an endless generator of memorable co-op moments.

Issy van der Velde: I've spent hundreds of hours in GTA Online, mostly using it as a vehicle to catch up with friends as we resupply each other's illicit businesses and chit chat about our lives. I enjoy it as a social space, one that exists on an invite-only server, but the chaos of the public ones is too infuriating for me. No thank you, Rockstar, I don't want to try and sell millions of dollars worth of drugs while people with unstoppable flying rocket bikes blow up hours of my hard work.

Released: August 8, 2018 | Top 100 Score: 225.33

Lincoln Carpenter: There are arguments to be made in favor of later Monster Hunter entries, but eight years after launch, World and its Iceborne expansion are—pound-for-pound—still the best encapsulation of Capcom's 20-year investment in making the most satisfying possible duels with the most charismatic possible dinosaurs. World was Monster Hunter's big budget introduction to a global market, and still feels like a celebration to match the occasion: a roster of excellent monster designs, some of the most vibrant maps in the series, and an admirable iteration of the 14 weapon types.

Sean Martin: And we all know that Insect Glaive is obviously the best of those iterations.

Released: August 21, 2007 | Top 100 Score: 226.00

Jake Tucker: BioShock is still one of the finest examples of how games can build a world that feels completely alive. Rapture’s crumbling art deco halls, eerie silence and unforgettable atmosphere create a setting you never want to leave. The combat is a perfect mix of guns, powers and experimentation, while its exploration of choice, control and ideology gives the whole adventure a weight few shooters have matched. It’s not just a great FPS, it's also an FPS that lets you blast a man in the face with an assload of bees.

Issy van der Velde: That twist made me rethink the way I engage with videogames entirely.

Andy Chalk: I'm sometimes tempted to give Ken Levine a hard time for making the same game over and over, but I can't complain too much about BioShock. The shooting and the politics are fine, but Rapture itself is the star—one of the most memorable videogame locales I've ever had the pleasure of exploring. I tend to be lukewarm on direct sequels but this is a notable exception: Tell me we're going back underwater to make sure Andrew Ryan's still dead and you can just have my money.

Sean Martin: Just a shame BioShock 2 is the better game, really. The more you learn about Rapture, the more you realise the city's story is best told through the perspective (and power fantasy) of a Big Daddy, not some dude who didn't even live there.

Jake Tucker: BioShock 2 is fine, but it struggles to justify its existence alongside the original. Rapture feels less mysterious the second time around, its philosophical ambitions are less compelling, and the story lacks the original’s devastating twists. Playing as a Big Daddy is fun, but familiarity ultimately diminishes the magic.

Issy van der Velde: I agree with both Jake and Sean here. The sequel lacks the wonder of the original, but it feels so much better to actually play. So, what do we value more? The story and immersion, or how it feels to blast splicers while dual wielding plasmids and a rivet gun?

Jake Tucker: Bioshock is on the top 100 list, and Bioshock 2 isn't, so…

Joshua Wolens: BioShock 2 is a game that conjures an entirely new, apparently vitally important character out of thin air just so it can do horseshoe theory with her and Andrew Ryan. But oh well, both 1 and 2 are epigones to the true greats: System Shock 1 and 2, which did everything the B'Shocks did but better.

Released: April 24, 2018 | Top 100 Score: 226.17

Sean Martin: I have just over 50 hours in Frostpunk, which is a hilariously short time for a game that's lived rent-free in my head for the past eight years. Though the city-building genre continues to endlessly innovate, Frostpunk's atmosphere and narrative leave an indelible mark, as you try to make good choices (and often don't) to shepherd your city through an icy apocalypse. It's not a game I'd hop into for fun, but it will etch itself into you forever… why am I recommending this, again?

Jake Tucker: The apex of the "failing is fun" genre, because you will fail in Frostpunk, no matter how hard you try. God, it's compelling though.

Released: October 24, 2017 | Top 100 Score: 226.43

Phil Savage: This year Destiny 2 ceased updates. It's no longer a live-service game. What we're left with, then, is arguably the best version of Bungie's shooter we've had in years. The final update was a triumph, removing the FOMO and seasonal uncertainty that has haunted Destiny 2 throughout its life. Now you get to focus on what was always the most important thing: exceptional gunplay, enjoyable buildcrafting and some of the most impeccably designed combat encounters and missions around. Destiny 2 is dead; long live Destiny 2.

Lincoln Carpenter: I hope I'm still this fun after I'm dead.

Sean Martin: There might be life left in it yet, too, with the campaign and raid content being unvaulted. Dare I hope for Destiny 3? (I daren't).

Fraser Brown: The best shooting in the worst game. I hope Destiny 2 sticks around forever because I enjoy seeing my colleagues having their hearts broken over and over again. I'm an awful person.

Andy Chalk: This is peak Remedy: Max Payne 2 goes for full pathos with a twisting tale of men and women clinging to each other for survival, purpose, and love as bullets scream, bombs blast, and blood flows from bodies broken like a weak man's dreams. Max's NYC is a perfect arena for balletic battles and Max Payne 2 packs them with guns, goons, and the poetic movement of bullet-time slo-mo. Shaun Prescott: There will never be agreement on which Yakuza game is the best, but there's something close to a consensus that Yakuza 0 is where you should start. This is the instalment that really took Ryu Ga Gotoku's longrunning Japanese crime melodrama to the western masses, not least because you don't need any knowledge of the other (checks Wikipedia) eight mainline games. RGG's commingling of gangster movie, Lynchian surrealism and goofy sentimentality is on full display here, and the combat is still sublime. Plus: karaoke rules.

Jody Macgregor: Karaoke totally rules. So do Kamarocho and Sotenbori, Yakuza 0's twin settings. Released: October 15, 2019 | Top 100 Score: 259.74

Ted Litchfield: Disco Elysium was the game that made me get serious about a career in games. It's now one of the biggest bummers I have to deal with professionally. The IP ownership and financial allegations? Byzantine. The interpersonal strife among its developers? Distressing. The layoffs and lives upended in its wake? To quote my man Geralt of Rivia, Poland's most soulful white boy from the previous entry on this list: It's "the last bitter drop in a chalice of sorrow."

And yet. Cut to the game underneath it all, and you'll still find a potentially life-changing work of baffling, miraculous provenance. Punks don't know how to make each other do the dishes without a struggle session. How the fuck did they make a game?

Six years on, it's easy to take Disco's design innovations for granted: Strip the so-so combat out of Planescape: Torment and replace it with a union of RPG and point 'n click adventure. Dialogue windows in the bottom-center of the screen with walls of text suck, so hammer it into a much more parsable, right-oriented vertical feed instead. Have the skills you invest in not only open opportunities, but shift the tone of the experience with their distinctive, hallucinatory personalities.

Disco tells a story with heart and characters that feel real, set in a tiny slice of a world that blends alternate history with pure fantasy like the best 20th century sci-fi writers, your Le Guins, Herberts, and Dicks. Its authors were people of strong social and political conviction who nevertheless trusted players enough to let them disagree and take the story in wildly different directions without it feeling like a failure state.

As I grow older, I've become more partial to stories that end. But we didn't get our fill of Elysium, and I still hope we can go back, someday.

Fraser Brown: A lot of the writing around Disco focuses on how weird it is, or how wonderful it is to have a videogame that's actually funny, and all of those things are true. But what really sticks with me is how heartbreaking it is. It's one of the only videogames to ever make my eyes get a bit leaky. Underneath all the high concept weirdness and political orienteering, it's an incredibly human game that hits like a fucking truck. We'll never see its like again.

Phil Savage: Heartbreaking, yes, but also hopeful. That's the thing that I wasn't expecting when I finally played it earlier this year. Maybe, if you work on yourself, you can find some meaning in that. Maybe the arthropods are in silent and meaningless awe of you.

Harvey Randall: While you're distracted thinking about everything said above, I'm going to take this chance to go on record and say that I want to marry Kim Kitsuragi. That is all.

This is one of the best ever RPG studios firing on all cylinders, building on decades of experience and experiments. I hope RPGs haven't peaked with BG3, but I'm struggling to imagine a future where this doesn't continue to be my favourite game of all time.

The prospect of adventure, the wonderfully written characters, and the endless twists and turns your journey takes amount to a truly unique gaming experience. Jody Macgregor: The Forgotten Realms isn't always an interesting backdrop for roleplaying, and I say that as someone who has run multiple campaigns there. Larian turned it into one by making the obligatory Realms stuff a delight—Volo the travelling disaster, Elminster the cheese freak—and pulling in cool bits from other D&D settings like githyanki and illithids so the world feels slightly alien and part of a larger cosmology. BG3 is a fantasy RPG through and through, but one that restores some of the genre's sense of wonder.

The thing that really makes it special is the reactivity. Act 3 is constantly referencing stuff you did in Act 1, and I only just found out if you take over the newspaper you can print your own stories, changing the city folk's ambient dialogue. Everything you do feels like it matters.

Ted Litchfield: 2023, '24, and much of '25 were dominated by BG3 for me, and it's been a second since I fired it up. I've been on a real Owlcat kick (we'll get Wrath of the Righteous or Rogue Trader on this list next year, prayer warriors), and when my favorite game is no longer right in front of me, my feckless heart can drift. Was it really that good?

Yes. Unequivocally. Universal heavyweight champion of the world. Just thinking about it for this write up has me wanting to roll a new guy⁠—I've never uninstalled, and I don't think I ever will barring force majeure. Larian simultaneously raised the bar on cinematic RPG storytelling while matching the crunchiest classics in depth and complexity. Common sense previously dictated that the two were mutually exclusive, and it feels like CRPGs can finally look forward, not back.

Harvey Randall: I have about 380 hours in this thing. I've completed it twice, once on honour mode, and I got another two extra honour mode playthroughs to Act 3 before I got distracted and left them in the dirt.

I can confidently call it one of the best RPGs that will perhaps ever be made. There's something about the sheer scope of it, the mixture of immersive sim style branching narratives and CRPG goodness that mashes up with professional, glossy production value and fully motion-captured cutscenes.

And while the TTRPG rules lover in me balks at Larian's irreverently-designed magic items which, let's be clear, grab D&D 5e's intended balance and snap it mercilessly over its knee… I'm still very glad they're there. They make the game a min-maxxer's delight.

Currently, I've been roped into an Honor Mode playthrough with Josh, Sean, and Ted, and my Cleric has stumbled onto a build that debuffs everybody just by standing around her. They can attest that I have made some utterly disgusting laugh-noises whenever I knock someone prone with Reverberation just for looking at me funny.

Surprise! There are more than 100 good videogames. Below you'll find a selection of individual recommendations—each a game that a member of the PC Gamer team thinks you should play.

Tyler Wilde, US Editor-in-Chief: Rocket League hasn't evolved much since 2015, but that's because it was already a perfectly-designed competitive team game which no one has yet improved upon. Playing soccer with rocket-powered cars has a high skill ceiling, but great teamwork can trump individual skill, which has led to some of the most exciting underdog wins of my gaming career. I'll be playing when I'm 80 if they don't turn the servers off before then.

John Strike, Senior Art Editor: Big pies. Flat beer. Crazy northeners. Drunk cows. Thank Goodness You’re Here! has it all and then some. This beautiful cartoon-style slapstick romp around the fictional and truly bizarre Yorkshire town of Barnsworth is a must-play for anyone with a soft spot for northern ways. Put your trousers on, grab your net and go and catch those spirit level bubbles!

Elie Gould, News Writer: Oh my god, I forgot to put Silent Hill f on the voting list. This is unforgivable considering how amazing it is and how well it managed to pave the way for the new kind of Silent Hill we're now seeing unfold. Its setting is chilling, mysterious, and cool as all hell, it gives us the best female protagonist I've seen in years, and we're tested with some seriously tricky puzzles and grotesque monsters. It's the whole package.

Christopher Livingston, Senior Editor: After a long absence I finally returned to Rare's open world ocean sandbox this year, and yep, there's still really no other game like it. The beauty of its world and water is still unmatched and there's nowhere else I've found that shares its blend of chill hangout vibes (90%) and humbling PvP nightmare (10%). All you can bring into each session are your skills because there's nothing else to give any pirate an advantage over another. One of a kind.

Rory Norris, Guides Writer: TESO is my most played game of all time, sitting at well over 2,000 hours in the decade since launch. It's an Elder Scrolls game but multiplayer, and it's been carrying the torch while the mainline series has been radio silent since Skyrim. You can explore almost all of Tamriel at this point, questing, doing world bosses, dungeons, and whatnot. And while it's technically a bit of a mess, the large-scale PvP is truly a sight to behold.

Ted Litchfield, Associate Editor: This one was supposed to be on the list proper, sorry everyone. Deadlock, I love you sweetie, but you're not finished. Step aside for what will be PCG's 2025 RPG of the year barring a coup and my execution. Esoteric Ebb riffs on Disco Elysium, but meaningfully pushes the evolving subgenre forward with smart changes like 6 attributes instead of 24 skills, potentially even greater reactivity⁠—especially in its handwritten turn-based battles⁠—and a comedic, hopeful, tone to set its excellent story apart.

Jody Macgregor, Weekend Editor: I may be a turn-based lover who sometimes thinks we should add Jagged Alliance to the Top 100, but even I know there have been a couple of classic RTSes, chief among them Dawn of War. It's got the best sense of scale of any game in the genre, a real feeling of ants versus bison as you build up to tanks and daemons, and the Definitive Edition lets you pull the camera back to appreciate it. Good luck, ants.

Joshua Wolens, News Writer: A 2024 narrative adventure that's more or less a visual novel, 1000xResist is one of those games that make you realise how narratively unambitious most other videogames are. It's about killing god, doing a revolution, inheriting trauma, inflicting trauma, the immigrant experience, the Hong Kong protests, original sin, noodles, and a lot else. It's like a modern Planescape: Torment, in that it's so tenderly and confidently written that it just makes all the other guys look bad.

Evan Lahti, Strategic Director: If you're an XCOM person with any affection for '80s/'90s action movies, JA3 should be your next game. It's campy, it's tropical, and your mercenaries (through story or tactical decisions) can find themselves in no-win scenarios. But my favorite detail is the simmy ballistics: bullets aren't just particle effects, they're physical objects that can scatter randomly and catch collateral hits against enemies, friendlies, civs, or scenery. The campaign itself is delightfully tabletop in its combo of scripted stuff and freedom.

Issy van der Velde, Deputy Editor, PC Gaming Show: Transistor has the best sci-fi love story I've ever experienced, and the combat is endlessly satisfying. Each ability can be used on its own, added to another to create a secondary effect, or held as a passive buff. It's easy to see how Supergiant built on this to create the boons in Hades. Everyone should play this masterpiece for Ashley Barrett and Darren Korb's soundtrack alone. There's even a dedicated button that lets you hum along to the music.

Phil Savage, Global Editor-in-Chief: If you like the idea of Blue Prince, but don't like the roguelike elements, then I have two things to tell you: 1) You are weak and need to fix yourself, and 2) you should play Lorelei and the Laser Eyes. Simogo's mystery box adventure is an absolute treat of puzzle design, cleverly laying out its challenges in cascading threads of discovery. It's deeply satisfying to solve both the individual puzzles and the building mystery of its story. A genuine treat.

Andy Chalk, US News Lead: The Plants vs. Zombies remaster that dropped in 2025 took some heat for technical shortcomings and allegations of AI art, but EA's addressed most of the complaints and these days it stands as a really good remaster of an all-time classic. The original is still available too, and much cheaper, and it holds up remarkably well for its age. Either way, Plants vs. Zombies is a short, snappy, incredibly cute and easy-to-engage tower defense game that remains as great—and essential—as ever.

Sean Martin, Senior Guides Writer: I'm unsure why my compatriots turned on Total War this year, but I'm here to remind you that Three Kingdoms is still incredible. Its quality is often overshadowed by its early demise, but it's quite unlike anything Creative Assembly ever made, or will likely make again. It channels the courageous characters, political machinations, and endless scheming of China's most culturally iconic period into a top-tier strategy game, achieving a harmonious balance between history and romance.

Andrea Shearon, Evergreen Writer: I've been enjoying the survival crafting renaissance, and by that I mean playing the hell out of Abiotic Factor and Enshrouded. The unbelievably detailed, massive high-fantasy RPG has one of the best building systems I've ever seen, and I love rescuing new villagers and crafters to slowly grow my own town. My only complaint is that Embervale is so pretty that I spend dozens of hours whispering, "Oh, maybe I'll settle down here," without getting anything done.

Morgan Park, Staff Writer: A gritty, unforgiving rally racing sim set in outer space. Exo Rally takes an already challenging rally format and adds gravity and thrusters into the mix. You'll tear your hair out trying to complete a singular turn on the moon, then ride the high of circumventing most of a track through well-timed thruster use. I haven't played enough yet to make my case for on the list, but it's turning me into a racing fan. A brilliant 2026 indie that's flying too low under the radar.

Mollie Taylor, Features Producer: I'm 13 years late to the party, but Project Zomboid's brutal, complex, and ridiculously moreish take on zombie survival has gripped me this year. It's one of the most customisable sandbox games I've ever tinkered with, meaning you can go for an unforgiving post-apocalyptic landscape or fine-tune it into a cosy (if not slightly gritty and terrifying) zombified The Sims 1. One of the few games I've been happy to sink hundreds of hours into learning.

Jacob Ridley, Managing Editor, Hardware: There are some games you can sink hour after hour into and not even realise it's already morning. Valheim is one of those games. Jump in with a couple of friends and build a new homestead, trying to one-up each other with ever more elaborate creations (our Sistine Chapel are two rival towers on top of massive rocks). Or just go exploring and hunt for new lands, hoping to survive the treacherous ocean journey. Yeah, it's a comfort game for me.

Andy Edser, Hardware Writer: Crimson Desert is not the ultimate action RPG, despite wearing the ambition proudly on its sleeve. But it's also the most fun I've had in a fantasy open world in years. The map is gigantic, and stuffed with bizarre details to explore. The combat is fiddly, yet satisfying to master. It's a game with obvious passion running underneath it, and a brilliant, bat-swinging attempt to make something with real scope and fresh ideas. More of this sort of thing, please.

Harvey Randall, Staff Writer: Perhaps a bit of a late entrant to catch PC Gamer's eye—which means I don't resent its absence from our Top 100 list—but I absolutely loved Mina the Hollower. It's a sprawling, satisfying Zelda-like with a bumping soundtrack and some of the best exploration I've had in a videogame. I was particularly impressed by how intuitive this game was. My experimentation-loving brain was constantly rewarded for putting its control scheme together in novel ways. Cute little mouse versus the eldritch horrors, what's not to love.

Fraser Brown, Online Editor: Big Walk launched after we created the magazine version of the Top 100 this year, otherwise I know it would have been in the list. This is simply the perfect co-op game. A simple, joyful puzzler absent a single flaw. Some of the antics its puzzles inspired genuinely left my crying with laughter, and that ending? Wow. It's a pure delight, start to finish. It's easily going to be my GOTY for 2026.

Phil has been writing for PC Gamer for nearly a decade, starting out as a freelance writer covering everything from free games to MMOs. He eventually joined full-time as a news writer, before moving to the magazine to review immersive sims, RPGs and Hitman games. Now he leads PC Gamer's UK team, but still sometimes finds the time to write about his ongoing obsessions with Destiny 2, GTA Online and Apex Legends. When he's not levelling up battle passes, he's checking out the latest tactics game or dipping back into Guild Wars 2. He's largely responsible for the whole Tub Geralt thing, but still isn't sorry.

#3708. Days Gone studio's next PlayStation exclusive to be revealed and released in 2027, according to new report

Sony's Bend Studio, perhaps one of its lesser discussed development houses, has apparently been deep in development on its next title. The game is reportedly set to be announced in 2027, and released in the same year.

That's according to MP1st, citing "people aware of what's happening at Bend". Like Days Gone, Bend's next game is in third-person. The title is said to include co-op support, but no live service elements.

The report doesn't say whether the game is based on a new IP or an existing one, but it does state that it's not a sequel to Days Gone. The game is apparently "much further along in development" than we realise, which isn't entirely surprising considering Bend has been quiet for years.

The seven years since the release of Days Gone in 2019 have been tumultuous for Bend Studio. The developer revealed in 2022 its next project is a new IP that "builds upon the open-world systems of Days Gone" and includes multiplayer elements.

Two years later, a job post described a game in development at Bend as a triple-A live service project. That unannounced game was then cancelled in 2025, triggering a wave of layoffs at the studio that took place a few months later. Bend hasn't said a word since then.

It's now clear the studio hopped on its next project following the cancellation of that live service game. Seeing as 2026 is nearly over, we're not likely to be waiting much longer to see that mysterious game unveiled.

#3707. How To Share Story Tips With Kotaku

Here at Kotaku, we strive to cut through the noise and nonsense and tell you real, interesting, and thought-provoking stories about the world of video games. In order to help us do that, we want people who know things about those video games and everything surrounding them to be able to talk to us securely and anonymously.

So weâve created a guide for anyone who wants to tip or share information with Kotaku, whether youâre a game developer, a customer service representative, a community leader, a PR representative, or a video game fan with a story to tell. The video game industry is shrouded in a culture of corporate silence that we do our best to penetrate every day, because we believe that people should have as much information as possible. So if you see or experience something that you think is important for people to know, or maybe just interesting, we want to hear from you, including in cases when you want your identity to be protected.

If you want to reach all of us, send your tips to: [email protected]

And if you want to send an e-mail to an individual Kotaku writer, find your favorite one on our masthead and shoot them a note.

Our tips inbox is only read by full-time staffers, and we check it every hour of every day. If you donât get a response, donât worry, weâve definitely seen it. And if you read this entire page and still arenât sure if you should send your tip, send it anyway. At worst, everyone at Kotaku will learn something new about the world of video games, and weâll be grateful for it.

But please do read the rest of the page first:

Weâre interested in news involving any aspect of gaming: game development, publishing, sales, things going on within games, things people are doing with games, all of it. Sometimes that means reporting on big cancelled projects or doing in-depth looks at chunks of video game history. Sometimes it means exposing malfeasanceâsharing stories about horrible work conditions at a game studio or reporting on a multinational company that isnât paying its staff on time. Sometimes it means answering big questions that everyoneâs asking, like why a game really keeps getting delayed over and over, or the events that led to a studio closure. We care about things that you yourself find interesting or surprising, and we want to help people know whatâs cool to play and what to avoid.

We primarily want gaming news, of course, and we care about it whether it comes from a gamer, a game-maker, or anyone else who gives a damn about video games. And if you have pictures, screenshots, video, or other first-hand evidence of whatever you want us to know about, thatâs a huge bonus.

We also, obviously, accept press releases, news about your cool indie game thatâs about to come out, pitches from PR to interview developers or preview or review games, and all the usual stuff. We recommend sending those to individual writers you have relationships with if possible, especially if you already know someone on staff is familiar with your game/genre/franchise. But if youâre just trying to reach us for the first time, the tips email is fine for that too.

Sometimes, you might want to share something with us, but want to remain anonymous because having your name attached to that information could come with consequences of some kind. Thatâs totally okay. In most cases, the journalist you speak to will still need to verify your identity (to prove youâd be in a position to know what youâre claiming to know), but will keep that information entirely to themselves if you prefer. We strictly do not share any information about anonymous sources with anyone for any reason.

In stories where we refer to sources who spoke to us anonymously, we will generally refer to those sources with as few details as possible. Often, that will just mean writing, âa source familiar with the matterâ or âan employee of [company]â or similar. Sometimes, some context clues will be necessary: for instance, if weâre writing about sexism at a studio, it may be important to identify the gender of our sources. We will always check with you first to make sure youâre comfortable with how youâre being referred to in the piece.

While we strictly do not share full articles with anyone outside of Kotaku prior to publication, we can on request go over your quotes with you after we speak to remind you of what was said and confirm there are no identifying details being used. We can also provide some general context about how the quotes are being used in the story, so you can help us confirm that our reporting is accurate to your understanding.

As a rule of thumb, you may not want to tell anyone that youâre talking to usâthe fewer people who know about any correspondence you may have with Kotaku, the more protected youâll be. Donât use your company e-mail account, any company-connected phone, work computer, or work WiFi network to contact us as an anonymous source. Instead, use a personal account or phone from home, or a public Wi-Fi network if you can do so safely. You can also reach most of our writers via Signal. Several of us have our Signal information in our social media bio pages, but if youâre looking for a specific writer, you can just email us directly and ask for our Signal name, no further context needed.

If the story youâd like to share with us would be improved by photos, screenshots, or other documentation, such records are often extremely helpful for us in corroborating a story and protecting your identity. If you can, itâs best to take pictures of photos or documents with a personal phone and send those, rather than the documents themselves. And when you send them to us, remove the metadata first. We do our own metadata scrubbing before we post leaked photos on Kotaku, but itâs best to be as safe as possible.

Similar to news tips, but different. While a lot of our stories are about game companies and creators, we also love writing about what gamers do.

Did you just play through Call of Duty without firing a shot? Are you one of the last dozen people playing the multiplayer in a game thatâs long since faded in popularity? Did you see someone pull off a crazy move in a Street Fighter tournament and happen to get video of it? Have you found a glitch no one knows about? Were you the person who figured out how to game the Steam summer sale? Did you make an incredible mod for your kids?

Maybe itâs not just you. Maybe youâve got a big Discord community dedicated to a game thatâs doing something neat. Or maybe youâre part of a subreddit thatâs very worked up about a niche update in the latest patch of your favorite game. Perhaps youâve got a local community putting on an in-person event surrounding something in a video game. Might be your guild in an MMO, your group chat, or maybe youâre still on forums.

We want to hear about all that stuff. Send it to tips. Send it to the staff. Just send it!

#3706. Remedy revenue soars by 226% following release of Control Resonant, the developer's fastest-selling game ever

Remedy - the developer behind the recently released Control Resonant - has released a scorcher of a quarterly financial report. It shows that following Resonant's release in September, the company's revenue surged by 226 percent, bringing in €39.6m in Q3.

This performance was described as "a defining milestone for the company" by CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon. The company reported a €0.6m operating profit this quarter, a fair leap upwards from the €16.4m loss from this time last year.

There are some interesting highlights to this sudden surging performance. For one, the US made up nearly half of Control Resonant's players across PC and console, followed by Chinese-speaking regions and then the UK.

Perhaps most crucially is that nearly half of Control Resonant's players were entirely new to the franchise, with the company stating: "Reaching new players was a key goal for this game, and these early results indicate a growing audience for the franchise and for Remedy."

Control (2019) also saw a bump up in sales thanks to the release of Control Resonant, showing a stronger performance this quarter than the past two quarters this year as well as its comparison period (this quarter last year).

Remedy's CEO now believes the focus for the studio is to "get Resonant into the hands of more players." He continues to say the game has provided a solid foundation for growth as other projects (including the Max Payne 1 & 2 remake) are in the works. In short, things appear to be looking rather good for Remedy.

Control Resonant was an artistically impressive but critically divisive game. While many praised the series' adventure into third person action, some felt it had less of a narrative bite than its predecessor. Nonetheless the game quickly blasted past one million sales after launch.
