Amazon’s long-gestating God of War show has arguably become one of the most discussed entries on the schedule of upcoming video game adaptations. The show hit a major setback earlier this year after lead actor Ryan Hurst was injured amid filming. Now, the show is restarting production, with Dave Bautista taking over for Hurst in the role of Kratos. Bautista has really been committing to the part and even gained 20 pounds of muscle to play it. To put it simply, the man looks jacked, and there’s a video that proves just that.

Those who’ve played the GoW video games are surely aware that Kratos – a deadly Spartan warrior – is a physically imposing character. So anyone who takes on the role would truly need to commit to gaining muscle. Considering the commitment Bautista has shown when playing roles of the years, it shouldn’t be surprising that he’s all in on training for Kratos. The fan-favorite actor recently took to his Instagram story to share a video of himself from the gym and make note of his 20-pound gain. DiscussingFilm also shared the clip to X:

Dave Bautista reveals he has gained 20 more pounds of muscle for playing Kratos in ‘GOD OF WAR’. He has now reached 250 pounds. https://t.co/fUOr0P7EABNovember 1, 2026

Man, those arms and pecs are serious! The Blade Runner 2049 star looks so swole, and it’s immediately clear to see that he’ll be able to manage the physicality of his God of War role. It goes without saying that Bautista is no stranger to training for roles, though, as this is the same man who worked to get super jacked to play Drax the Destroyer from the Marvel Cinematic Universe. His level of work is well known, and it was even a motivating factor for Jason Momoa (his The Wrecking Crew co-star).

What’s particularly interesting about all this is that it comes just a few years after Bautista’s comments on a pivot of sorts in his career. The A-lister previously talked about taking a step away from action-related fare due to no longer being “the great, big, muscular guy [he] used to be.” Said comments also coincided with a point at which the My Spy star began to slim down a bit from his typically ripped physique. While Bautista opined that he wouldn’t get acting roles into his 50s, God of War has proven the 57-year-old star wrong on that front.

Of course, the fact that Dave Bautista landed the role of Kratos following an unfortunate set of circumstances should be ignored as well. It was in January 2026 that Ryan Hurst was announced to be playing the role and, in February, Prime Video released the first still of him as the character. In July 2026, it was reported that Hurst – who put on 40 pounds of muscle for the job – tore his biceps while filming a stunt and that due to the length of his predicted recovery time, his role would have to be recast.

The Dune alum’s casting was announced in August 2026 and many expressed excitement over Bautista playing Kratos. The show is set to focus on Kratos and his son, Atreus (Callum Vinson) as they seek to spread the ashes of Faye, their wife and mother in a specific spot within the nine realms. It’s been reported that filming either has restarted or will ramp up again in the coming days. Four episodes were reportedly shot before Hurst’s exit, and they’ll have to be completely redone due to Vinson having aged a bit.

While it’s still early, it’s already been confirmed that GoW is getting a second season as well. If the show proves to be a success, this could end up being another role that Dave Bautista plays for an extended period of time. That’ll certainly be some serious work for him, especially given what’s required for a show of this magnitude. However, if Bautista’s workout video conveys anything, it’s that he has some serious drive and can continue to deliver as an actor from a physicality standpoint.

A release window has yet to be announced for God of War, so fans will want to keep their eyes peeled on that. In the meantime, anyone who wants to stream the show when it finally arrives should grab a Prime Video subscription.

#3704. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.

The long-awaited title of the next Elder Scrolls game was revealed in a video marking Bethesda Softworks' 40th anniversary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Eight years after it was announced, it's finally officially official: The next RPG in Bethesda's long-running Elder Scrolls series is called Sentinel.

The title was revealed in a video celebrating Bethesda's 40th anniversary, narrated by Todd Howard (of course), who cast back to the studio's first game, Gridiron—Bethesda was big on sports games back in the day—before moving into The Elder Scrolls series, the games that would take it to the big leagues, in the early 1990s.

"As we're here in the 40th anniversary, we think about all of the games we've made," Howard says as the video draws to an end.

"And so even though yes, we're looking back,we're also looking forward to all we're doing, particularly with the Fallout franchise and obviously The Elder Scrolls. You know, everybody's always asking about Elder Scrolls 6. And we thought, hey, given the moment, what a perfect time to tell you what The Elder Scrolls 6 is actually called."

And thus is the title revealed: Sentinel.

There's an interesting quote after the title is revealed: "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." Those words were uttered by Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell in the year 4E 206, which was UESP pointed out puts Sentinel at least five years after the events of Skyrim.

No other details are revealed, but the title (and that quote) presumably also reveals the setting: Hammerfell, home of the redguards. Sentinel itself is one of Hammerfell's major kingdoms and capital of the Alik'r Desert—reflected in the teaser's sandy backdrop. It's something of a geographical shift from the flyover of the generic mountains seen in that 2018 reveal, although the Alik'r is bordered by the Dragontail Mountains, so who knows.

But, for those who like to dig deep in search of clues, here's the best image I could get of the jewelled whatsit revealed under the sand, just before it disappears. Mean anything to you?

So there you have it! The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel. Hopefully it won't take another eight years before we hear anything more about it.

#3702. It looks like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 had fewer active players at launch in the US compared to last year's Black Ops 7

It's been speculated for a while that Call of Duty may be losing its lustre. Although we don't have concrete data with detailed statistics for each game released in the last several years, there's an observable trend in player numbers that's hard to ignore.

US market analysis firm Circana published some data showing player engagement with Modern Warfare 4 following its launch, and compared them to those by Black Ops 7.

The data is based on Circana's proprietary Player Engagement Tracker, which tracks player activity in the US across Steam and PlayStation, and worldwide on Xbox. According to Circana analyst Mat Piscatella, 19 percent of players on PlayStation played Modern Warfare 4 in the week ending 24th October, compared to 17 percent on Xbox, and 4.2 percent on Steam.

With the exception of Steam, those numbers are down compared to last year's Black Ops 7, which saw 23 percent engagement on PlayStation, 29 percent on Xbox, and a meagre 1.5 percent on Steam during its launch week.

Call of Duty managed to land in the top 10 across all three platforms during the same week ending 24th October, per Circana. In fact, it sat just below Fortnite on PlayStation, which is a decent result.

The large drop in activity on Xbox could be explained by Modern Warfare 4's lack of a day-one release on Game Pass. Black Ops 7 was the second (and last) Call of Duty to launch on Game Pass day-and-date with its premium release. Game Pass availability typically boosts player numbers, though not always sales.

The drop on PlayStation is a little harder to explain, but could be a side effect of the incredibly successful Black Ops 1 & 2 ports released in the summer on PS4 and PS5, which captured lapsed players who may have simply lost interest in modern Call of Duty, regardless of the perceived quality of Modern Warfare 4.

Judging by the data we have access to, such as SteamDB numbers showing Modern Warfare 4's launch compared to Black Ops 7's and other recent releases, there's evidence this year's game perhaps isn't as popular as it could've been.

Indeed, even Activision's tenor when talking about Call of Duty first weekend sales has changed. The publisher issued a single statement following Modern Warfare 4's launch, through Xbox CEO Asha Sharma, which does not even mention the game by name.

"One of the most celebrated Call of Duty games in its 24-year history, and now $40bn in lifetime franchise revenue," Sharma wrote on X. "An incredible milestone. Congrats to the Activision team. And to the players, thank you for being with us."

Last year's Black Ops 7 post-launch statement sidestepped talk of sales and revenue entirely, insteading praising the "great response to the quality and depth of gameplay in Black Ops 7".

#3701. Fan Who Went Viral Wishing To Stay Alive Long Enough To Play GTA 6 Has Passed Away

Jerry Fort, the GTA VI fan who went viral on TikTok for expressing his hope to live long enough to play the game, has passed away. As reported by Dexerto, his family confirmed the sad news, announcing that he passed on October 29th after complications following lung transplant surgery.

Earlier this year, Fort posted a video from his hospital bed titled “I just want to play GTA VI” in which he detailed his situation and prognosis. The video quickly went viral, garnering millions of views and tens of thousands of comments wishing him a speedy recovery and urging Rockstar Games to get in touch to make his wish come true. His family put up a Gofundme to raise money for a lung transplant and it quickly blew through its original $15,000 goal to reach over $100,000.

Fort and occasionally his sister posted regular updates to his account informing his followers of his progress, and it generally seemed like he was improving. In September, Fort went in for lung transplant surgery. After the surgery he developed an infection and after fighting the infection for several weeks, declining to go into hospice care, he finally succumbed.

After his plea to make it to GTA VI went viral, he put out a video thanking people for their support, promising to stream the game when he fully recovered. “That’s gonna be our goal as a community.”

Spoilers ahead for the Season 4 premiere of The Gilded Age.

Shortly after its premiere, The Gilded Age joined the ranks of HBO shows that got the world talking. Luckily for fans of the period piece, Season 4 has finally arrived on the network (and streaming with a HBO Max subscription). While the show sometimes gets flak online for not having enough drama, I'll admit the premiere episode had me biting my nails for two different reasons. Let's break it all down.

It remains to be seen if The Gilded Age finally gets a Downton Abbey crossover, but Season 4 started off with a bang. The premiere was titled "Ring the Bells" and put two major characters in peril.

The first of which was Louisa Jacobson's Marian Brook. After attending the after party of Oscar van Rhijn and Enid Winterton's wedding, Marian gets into a carriage with Larry Russell. The horse gets spooked by the storm, starts running out of control. I really thought they were going to get into an accident, but it turns out that the real "danger" was Marian losing her inhibitions and the pair sleeping together at a hotel. She's now worried about the news getting out, and her reputation (and chances at marriage) being ruined forever. Different set of stakes, but I'll take it.

Then there was the drama with Taissa Farmiga's Gladys. She was shown struggling to give birth in the Season 4 premiere, and I thought for a minute that the character might end up being killed off. The stakes got even higher when she started hemorrhaging from the breech birth, and let's just say that I didn't have faith in the medicine of 1880s enough to save her life.

Luckily both she and her young son survived the birth, but not without sacrifice. The doctor ended up performing a hysterectomy to save her life, meaning that she (obviously) can no longer get pregnant. While not life-threatening, but potentially puts her marriage to The Duke in jeopardy. If something happens to their child he might be inspired to find another wife who can help produce an heir.

Fans want a number of Gilded Age characters to make a splash in Season 4, and it should be interesting to see how things play out. The Gilded Age Season 4 already seems like its making some big changes to the beloved series, and I'm eager to see how things shake out over the next few months.

The Gilded Age airs new episodes Sundays on HBO as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Folks who thought the show doesn't have enough drama might want to tune back in and see if they change their mind.

World of Warcraft's big crossover with Dungeons & Dragons is finally here—and despite being a huge flagship collaboration, one of the biggest MMOs meeting with one of the biggest TTRPGs, I'm sad to say I'm feeling just a touch whelmed. This sourcebook is inconsistent—filled with very cool character options in some places, and just pointing at the already-existing player's handbook in others.

That inconsistency doesn't let the whole project down, mind. There are still some rules tucked away in here that I think are great additions to any campaign, not just a World of Warcraft-themed one.

Let's start with the big one: Classes. WoW and D&D do have a lot of overlap in terms of class fantasy—there's not much in the way of appreciable differences between a Fighter and a Warrior, other than a few iconic abilities being missing from the pack. As a result, this rulebook essentially uses the pre-existing classes as a template to throw some WoW flavour on.

Some of these changes are meaningful—take, for example, the Death Knight. This uses the Paladin's chassis, but throws in a ton of impactful changes, replacing Lay on Hands with Death Coil, for example. It also throws a whole new raft of Death Knight-adjacent spells, adjusts your Find Steed with a cool undead ghost that can phase through objects, and more.

A lot of the classes are solved by custom spells like this—the Paladin, for instance, has just the one new subclass to cover for Holy and a bunch of iconic Paladin spells. But the balance of these is a touch skewiff in places. Take Divine Shield, for instance. This thing is straight busted.

It's a 4th level spell, which does admittedly mean you'll only get it at levels 13 plus, but it makes you immune to not only the damage of a triggering attack, but also all damage until the start of your next turn. AND you can't be moved or have your speed reduced. While absolutely correct for the flavour of WoW's iconic bubble, this is crazy overpowered.

And while some of these classes do have a lot new on offer, others are so thin on content it's a wonder why they're there at all. The rogue gets a particularly short end of the stick, for instance. Outlaw rogues are just given a reskinned version of 5e's Swashbuckler subclass (which does, in fairness, have some new Cunning Strike options to bring it up to parity). Otherwise, the book just points you in the direction of pre-existing subclasses.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Others are a complete miss, too. Shamans are all awkwardly stuffed into the chassis of the Barbarian, which only really works for Enhancement shamans—Elemental and Restoration shamans are pretty much just your standard D&D barbarian with some flavour-adjacent rage options, rather than the full spellcasters they are in the videogame.

This inconsistency in quality applies to character origins, too. Some of them have fully bespoke traits—Dracthyr get their visage forms, Void Elves get this cool void form that triggers when you hit identical numbers on an Advantage/Disadvantage roll, and so on. And then there are Orcs and Dwarves, some of WoW's most iconic races, where the book goes: Just use the stuff that's already in the PHB.

And yet, there's a lot to this supplement I actually like. When it's actually adding new options to the classes, I think they're cool—the Frost Mage flavoured feat, Fingers of Frost, gives you extra cold damage against restrained creatures, for example. But the real thing I would encourage you to just crib for your non-Azerothian games are its gathering and crafting systems.

In 5e (and the 2024 rules), crafting's always been sort of a joke. There are tool proficiencies, but they might come up every once in a blue moon. The actual Player's Handbook just says to half the cost of an item, then smacks you around the head with a massive downtime cost for anything particularly expensive—a suit of plate armor takes a whopping 150 days to craft (though you can split this with extra help). At which point you might as well just eat the GP cost and buy the damn thing.

This book, however, has some really neat rules for gathering and crafting professions. Having the right tool proficiency gives you access to a profession, which you can level up when your proficiency bonus increases to new tiers (which also increases the rarity of the items you can make).

Instead of making players shell out the gold cost, these gathering professions have a neat little table for getting enough golds' worth in raw materials to make the thing, with extra bonuses for beating the involved DC by five or more. When you get to higher levels, certain recipes might require items from specific regions—and you might only know how to make those items via recipes obtained from certain factions.

It's still all pretty lightweight (although each profession does have a useful list of suggested recipes it should know) but that's honestly a boon to this system, rather than a bane, because you could very easily just slot this whole mechanic into your homebrew campaign with very little trouble.

And, more to the point, you could very easily make entire adventure hooks out of going to get specific materials for a recipe here—which helps solve D&D crafting's main issue: It's not relevant unless you have literal months of in-game downtime to kill. While the book doesn't make changes to the time-to-craft issue, it's still a major step up.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent."

Renown's another mechanic I like. You get renown with certain factions based on your origins, but you can increase this renown through play to get certain perks. For instance, improved renown with Darnassus gives you the option to learn certain proficiencies, gain a blessing from its leaders, or gather extra materials with herbalism. My favorite of these is the gnomeregan Shield Guardian perk, which specifically states that if you dip below 50 renown again, the guardian turns on you. Sorry buddy, my creator says you dropped off.

Aside from these rules additions, there are also some solid dungeon adventures with their own bespoke stat blocks, extra magic items, and a respectable bestiary full of critters to toss into your campaign.

The fact that there's plenty to like in this book makes it all the more frustrating that it's so inconsistent—some areas have novel, if a little wonky, additions to the system. Others shrug like the book's designers simply ran out of time and budget, pointing towards resources that you already own.

However, if you are looking to run a WoW-specific campaign, or just want crafting rules that don't suck, it very well might be worth checking out on the strength of its secondary mechanics alone. Just don't go in there expecting a 1:1 replication of the MMORPG. This is still Dungeons & Dragons—and in some places, I mean that literally.

#3698. Indie game website itch.io expands its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' continues to overwhelm Steam and other storefronts

Indie game storefront itch.io has expanded its AI disclosure filters, allowing its users to better separate games made with the controversial technology from those who don't.

This expansion, revealed on its official BlueSky account, includes Itchio's search page which now features a "No AI" box. By ticking this, users can hide any game on the website that features the generative AI disclosure. Games created using generative AI must have this disclosure to be present on the platform, similarly to Steam, although without an option to describe to what extent the tech was used.

This change comes shortly after itch.io also revealed the number of game pages being made on the website each day had doubled in the past two months. And, of course, the number of games downloaded and purchases have not doubled to match this new supply.

itch.io is also facing issues linked to the sheer file size. The storefront has a terms of service policy against AI spam, which it cited shortly after it publicly announced "a couple terabytes of AI slop" had been deleted.

This change comes as the industry as a whole has been clogged with an influx of AI games. Steam Next Fest had a record-breaking number of demo submissions last month. Developers pulled demos in fear of their game being copied, and with Steam saying it's the developer's responsibility to make their games less copyable.

It's an issue that isn't going away any time soon. Even as Claude creator Anthropic has introduced rules preventing unoriginal game clones, alternative AI tools can still be used to create them, and the process of creating games using AI tools will still allow for hastily made, low effort slop. Perhaps filters, like the one itch.io has expanded, is a workable solution to this on-going problem.

#3696. COD: Modern Warfare 4 DMZ patch has nerfed UAV Towers so you're not immediately visible everywhere you go

The Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 patches continue, with the latest delivering some big changes to the game's extraction mode DMZ. The latest hotfix introduced a key balance change to one of DMZ's most controversial mechanics: UAV Towers.

UAV Towers, previously guaranteed to spawn in every Point of Interest (POI) in the map, have now had their spawn logic randomised. Infinity Ward also reduced their spawn rate by 40 percent, meaning you're less likely to find them across the various regions of the map. As noted in the patch notes, that change also prevents multiple towers from spawning the same area. The only exception is the Deadtown area, which factors into DMZ Order progression and requires multiple towers.

By taking away the guarantee that each POI will have at least one UAV Tower, the patch removes one of the core tactics PvP-inclined and aggressive players have been relying on since DMZ's launch. It's common for players to spawn in, and immediately run around activating as many UAV Towers as possible to reveal the movement of enemy players, even if they're not interested in directly engaging them.

Indeed, some of the UAV Towers cover extraction areas, so it's easy for players intending to ruin the day of others as they're extracting to set up elaborate traps. Making matters worse, a particular character trait prevents UAV Towers from expiring, allowing the scans to stay up for the entire match.

Infinity Ward has not commented directly on that trait, but the developer confirmed it's being changed so the Sedative Inhaler - which hides you from UAVs - also works with those trait-upgraded towers, though that change won't arrive until sometime in Season 1.

Finally, today's update further makes it easier to stay undetected by boosting the Sedative Inhaler's duration to 120 seconds, double that of the previous 60, which should help while we wait for larger changes to be implemented.

DMZ has been one of Modern Warfare 4's most discussed modes online. Recently, players discovered what appears to be a separate matchmaking pool for Story Missions that prevents solo sessions from featuring other players, though with some caveats.

Konami might have finally set down the Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol 1 to focus on releasing Metal Gear Solid 4 from its PS3 prison, but modders continue chipping away at the PS2-and-earlier era Metal Gear games. MGSHDFix, whose mission statement is to repair broken visual bugs, fix crashes, and generally give the older Metal Gears a bit of a spitshine, has got a big new update. Now is the era of MGSHDFix 5.0 (actually, 5.0.1. There was a hotfix).

"We've got performance improvements, massive vanilla loading time reductions for MGS2, loose .MP3/.WAV/.OGG/FLAC soundtrack loading for MG1/MG2, WIP raw mouse input support, and loads of new restoration and bugfixes", writes author Afevis Solmunko.

There are, to be honest, way too many fixes to properly delve into here, so I recommend either checking the patch notes out yourself or taking the mod for a spin in your preferred Metal Gear. We can call out some of the big ones, though.

For example, want to play Metal Gear 2 as Mel Gibson? No? Well that's a shame, bucko, because MGSHDFix 5.0 provides an option to restore that game's MSX2 sprites. "Yes, you can finally experience Mel Gibson fighting Sean Connery as Kojima intended," writes Solmunko.

Also in the OG MGs, there's now an option "to make doors automatically check your inventory for keycards (how MGS2 keycards work)", which frankly sounds blasphemous to me.

More practically, the latest version of the mod boasts that it dramatically cuts down loading times in MGS2. "We've greatly sped up level loading by adding a new system that prefetches a list of all the assets for all the rooms that are directly connected to the current stage you're in… Speedrunners have reported that this new prefetch system has shaved upwards to 5 minutes off of the elapsed realtime from their runs". On Linux (and thus, Steam Deck) specifically, Solmunko says this can "reduce level transitions load times by 4~6 seconds for every room you go into".

Plus, MGS2 and MGS3 now have limited support for raw mouse input in third-person, with support for first-person hopefully coming in MGSHDFix 5.1.0.

#3694. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel is confirmed, finally getting new trailer and full name, 8 years, 4 months, and 23 days after its reveal

Today, Xbox and Bethesda have finally revealed the name and more information about The Elder Scrolls 6. The game, which we now know carries the subtitle Sentinel, was revealed in a special video that took place today, 3rd November 2026, almost exactly 15 years since the launch of The Elder Scrolls 5: Skyrim and eight years, four months, and 23 days since the first reveal of the title card for The Elder Scrolls 6. That's over 100 months, by the way, or 3067 days, if you want to get specific.

In the trailer, a glimpse of the new game - mostly with some fancy sand physics - before the name, Sentinel, is revealed formally. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes. A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate," says a quote in the video, attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell.

"For 40 years, we've explored new worlds, told unforgettable stories, and gone on incredible adventures together," says a blurb for new video. "From everyone at Bethesda Game Studios, thank you for joining us along this journey, for making these worlds your own, and for inspiring us to keep creating. Here's to 40 more."

This reveal comes after a report last week suggested we'd be seeing more of the highly-anticipated fantasy RPG in November, and which also predicted the name of the game. That report suggested that the title will take place in the Tamriel region of Hammerfell, will touch on the "history of the Elder Scrolls" and will "help uncover the secrets of these mysterious ancient artifacts". This trailer seems to confirm all that.

Asha Sharma, CEO of Xbox, said she'd played the game in August on a trip to the Bethesda offices, as a giant inflatable rat and a union protest took place outside. Notably, the reveal of the game is taking place not six months after Bethesda suffered sweeping job cuts (alongside many other Microsoft-owned studios) as part of Xbox's "reset".

So why has it taken eight years for Bethesda to show us this game? Previously, Skyrim's lead designer Bruce Nesmith noted that the studio and boss Todd Howard felt pressured to reveal the game to the world because "the pitchforks and torches were out". "[...] Todd's opinion - one which I share, by the way - is that the video game industry has short memories," he said in an interview in 2023. "Those companies that start touting their games years ahead of time, actually, you know, they screw themselves. The best time to start talking about it is six months before release." It's worth noting, then, that this is what Bethesda did with Fallout 4.

Does that hint at a timeline for more Sentinel footage being shown soon, and a potentially sooner-than-we-thought release date? Who knows. If we are going to see the game again anytime soon, it's most likely going to be during The Game Awards 2026, which is taking place on 10th December.

It's clear Julia Stiles is on the elimination bubble of Dancing With The Stars, after guest judge Shirley Ballas gave her a 4 on Halloween Night. While there's always a chance for competitors to bounce back after an off week, I think her song choice for Disney Night is only going to help her get sent home this week.

The song list for Disney Night dropped ahead of the annual episode on the 2026 TV schedule, and there are some questionable picks. Julia and Ezra Sosa's choice might be the strangest of them all, because I think plenty of fans will have something to say about a Hamilton song slipping through.

I know that Disney loves to remind us that Hamilton is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription, but it is not a stage production that originated from the House of Mouse. I'm sure that's why Julia and Ezra were allowed to pick "Satisfied" for their upcoming performance, but that doesn't make it any less aggravating.

There are too many good Disney movies to include a song from a project that doesn't originate from the studio. While it's true that contestants and pros have limited control over the songs they get during a season via a questionnaire, clearly that had to fill out something that ranked it high on the list to get it. Is Dancing With The Stars' Disney night just another vehicle for the company to cross-promote its other brands? Absolutely, but including a dance number for something that isn't inherently from it really kills the vibe.

It feels like the writing is on the wall for Julia Stiles on Dancing With The Stars. Now that viewers have seen her pay homage to Save The Last Dance as well as her tribute to Heath Ledger, they're now more concerned about her actual dancing.

I'm Watching Dancing With The Stars For The First Time, And Now I Am All In

Stiles had a standout performance with her contemporary dance and scored all nines. That said, when it comes to more traditional dances, she's struggled tremendously and hovered toward the bottom of the leaderboard most of the competition.

With the exception of Tatyana Ali, the rest of the Dancing With The Stars contestants are leaps and bounds ahead of her. Just from talking to various people who are watching this season, there seems to be a growing desire to keep Tatyana in the competition and let Julia's run come to an end.

We're deep into DWTS Season 35, so it's inevitable that favorites are going to go home. Only the best of the best should be in the finale, and if they aren't, the audience and judges have failed. As such, I think it's curtains for Julia this week, unless she puts on a truly stellar performance.

Disney Night is on ABC and Disney+ on November 2nd. Make note of the fact that it's a Monday night, as network television will be taken over by the midterm election results.

#3690. Nintendo Rehired One Of The Original Voice Actors For The Ocarina Of Time Remake Without Even Realizing It

NintendoThe Legend of ZeldaThe Legend of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time

Fans have been speculating for a while now that the original voice of Navi, Kaori Mizuhashi, is returning to reprise her role in the Japanese cast of the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake. While Nintendo still hasn’t confirmed that, it has confirmed that at least one actor is returning from the original, and what’s more, the game’s design leads had no idea they were rehiring the same person until they’d made the decision.

The latest Ask the Developer interview from Nintendo talks about Ocarina of Time‘s music and sound with sound director and music lead Masato Ohashi. Ohashi first talks about the sound, saying that the team composed new music to go with a lot of the game’s new cutscenes, adding up to over 150 pieces of background music in total.

At one point, he says that some pieces “combine a live full orchestra with sounds from the original Nintendo 64 version,” then goes on to clarify that “[w]e didnât use the audio output from Nintendo 64 as is. Instead, we used the original Nintendo 64 sound source as a reference to faithfully recreate some of the sounds. We wanted to do something only Nintendo could as a way of bringing back memories of that time.”

Link’s house music is offered as an example of this, with a snippet of the new track embedded in the interview. I’ll be honest, I’m struggling to understand exactly what he means here, because I don’t hear any of the sounds from the original track in the new one. I think what’s being said is that they listened to the original sound source (before any of the sound was processed through the N64) and then recreated some of those sounds for the remake, but I’d happily hear from audiophiles in the comments if I’m misunderstanding it, and I’ve asked Nintendo for comment.

Ohashi goes on to talk about layering in more subtle sounds, like leaves rustling or water running over rocks, to fill out the world. The ocarina songs are played from recordings of a real ocarina, so you can hear the breathiness to it.

“This game supports 5.1-channel surround sound, making the sounds of the game world feel more three-dimensional. Even without a home theater setup, you can experience the gameâs rich ambient sound in Kokiri Forest and many other locations by connecting headphones to your Nintendo Switch 2 system. I hope youâll give it a try.”

But the bit that stood out to me the most was the conversation about voice actors. Fans already suspected that the original Navi had rejoined the Japanese cast of the game for the remake, even as the English version gets a new Navi voice. While the team stops short of confirming that Kaori Mizuhashi is back for the remake, director HokWai Ng confirms that the team did conduct totally blind auditions for all the roles, with the top priority being to pick “voices that recreated the sound and feel of the original game.” Eiji Aonuma adds that they deliberately hid the voice actors’ names during the Japanese auditions, “[a]nd as fate would have it, one of the actors we selected had actually voiced the same character in the Nintendo 64 version. None of us saw that coming.”

I’m just trying to imagine being Mizuhashi and showing up for a voice audition for a role I’d performed 28 years ago, trying to nail the performance by making it as close to the original as possible, and obviously slam-dunking it. God, what if she hadn’t been cast? There’s always a (slim, admittedly) chance Aonuma is referring to someone else. Did any other original voice actors show up and not get picked? Yikes?

Indie-oriented digital storefront Itch.io is beginning to push back against the rising flood of AI, announcing on social media that it's "deleted a couple terabytes of AI slop" and made it easier for users to filter out games made with generative AI.

A few days after Valve admitted that Steam has a problem with AI slop and game cloning, Itch.io chimed in to say it's experiencing something very similar: The number of game pages being created every day on the storefront has doubled over the past two months.

Itch.io didn't provide a reason for the phenomenon, but it's not hard to figure out: When one Bluesky asked why it was happening, Itch.io replied "take a guess," accompanied by crying and robot smilies, and then added that "the number of downloads and purchases has *not* doubled."

Now it seems to be moving to action. "Just deleted a couple terabytes of AI slop," the storefront posted last night. "Just because you can upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models doesn't mean you should upload 10 terabytes of poorly optimized AI generated models."

The account also linked to Itch.io's guidelines on "uploading excessive amounts of automatically generated or AI-generated content," which says that while content created by generative AI "can be useful or interesting, do not use automated systems to mass produce product pages. We will consider this spam and may remove your pages from our browse and search pages."

The guidelines apply to, but are not limited to:

Like Steam, Itch.io requires developers and publishers to disclose their use of generative AI in their games. That disclosure requirement has now been expanded from game assets to "the tabletop (aka physical games), books, comics and soundtracks categories," all of which now require disclosure.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It has also added new browsing and search filters on the site, so users can exclude some or all use of generative AI.

The tabletop (aka physical games), books, comics and soundtracks categories on itchio now require completing an AI disclosure in order to edit or create your page. These join the game assets section which has required disclosure for the past 2 years.

The "No AI" tag page cuts straight to it:

Itch.io's action isn't likely to stem the tide of AI slop that's engulfing the world of gaming. Apart from the fact that it represents a very small percentage of a market dominated by Steam, the simple truth is that AI slop is easy to churn out in overwhelming quantities—that's what makes it so attractive to people who care less about creation than they do about making a few bucks on a lucky swing of the bat.

But it is action, and I think that's important: While some argue that mandatory AI disclosures have the potential to harm developers, the gen AI geyser is unquestionably doing harm right now, to users, developers, and the industry as a whole. Unless and until that changes, proactively excising the worst of the slop torrent and making it easier for gamers to avoid the mess entirely is the least that online storefronts can do.

#3688. Arc Raiders devs say that using generative AI voice acting was necessary as actors "would just go crazy if they had to read all of that"

CCO states: "We are not in the industry of replacing actors.".

Developers at Embark Studios, the company behind Arc Raiders, have spoken on the use of generative AI voice acting in the extraction shooter. It's argued that the initial use of generative AI line reads was a benefit to the voice actors, as they: "would just go crazy if they had to read all of that".

This comes from a recently released video by Embark, focused on Arc Raider's sound and music. In it, several key members of staff speak on the game's use of generative AI, be it the initial use of it for voice lines, and the gradual replacement of it with human line reads.

Audio director Bence Pajor first spoke about the struggles he ran into at previous studios; how gameplay decisions couldn't be changed because voice lines were already locked in. He describes this as a "true pain", and that it places stress on the writing team, dialogue team, and voice actors who may have scheduling clashes. He said that using reachable voice actors in Stockholm, and using the tools available, made life easier for everyone.

Later in the video, Pajor explained that training data was made with the voice actor's performances. Due to the voice lines being required for each new feature, item, or weapon added into the game, he argues it would be too impractical to record every possible version of a line read. "The actors would just go crazy if they had to read all of that," Pajor said.

Pajor continues by pointing to Arc Raider's many updates and changes since its release in October 2025, it would be impractical to call in voice actors to record lines every time an altered line read needed to happen. Two voice actors present in the video - Jo Rideout (Shani) and Diana Gardner (Celeste) - also shared their feelings on it. Gardner said it was "freeing" that she could take a job somewhere else, without worrying about cancelling other shoots or projects.

However, Gardner would later speak on the topic of her ownership of Celeste's many lines in the game: "The contract seemed so fair [...] so it was a no-brainer in that sense. But I didn't know what to expect once I heard the voice come out. I was like, 'Can I take ownership for the performance?' [...] This is hours of work that I've put in, but can I take ownership for the final product? No."

Even with these proposed benefits to using AI-powered performances, these voice lines are being replaced. Embark CCO Stefan Strandberg said: "we are not in the industry of replacing voice actors", and acknowledges that immersion-breaking experiences many players had when playing Arc Raiders and hearing these performances. Strandberg and Pajor both admit to understanding the AI critique, and point to the work being done to replace what they can.

"We are not in the industry of replacing actors," said Strandberg. "Actually I think quite the opposite. We should celebrate the performance and give them more space. That's something I'm hoping to give to players over the coming years."

Part of this critique over generative AI's use in Arc Raiders came from reviews, including our own. Embark Studios faced similar pushback for gen-AI voice acting in The Finals, however Arc Raider's popularity while using the technology led Nexon to describe it as a "trojan horse" for gen AI's use in small team game development.

I don’t know what’s going on with the Survivor edit. I’m not saying fans can always tell who is going to win halfway through every season, but typically at this point, there are two or three strong contenders who more educated fans have coalesced around. That’s definitely not the case at this point in 51. Everyone is still all over the island with their predictions, and there’s perhaps no better example of that than Kristin Flickinger.

Arguably the most universally liked contestant on 51 with the possible exception of Ori, Kristin has probably gotten the most consistently positive edit of any player. Every single time she’s on the screen, the editors seem invested in making her look good. We got a segment where she showed off her negotiation skills. We got a segment where we saw her winning over her tribemates after the swap. We’ve gotten multiple segments where she showed off her literal survival skills. We’ve gotten confessionals where she’s detailed all the strong relationships she has on the island. We even got a montage of all of her audition tapes over the years.

It’s the kind of edit Survivor players dream about getting, but is it a winner’s edit? Well, fans and so-called Edgic experts are not on the same page at all. Some see her as overwhelmingly the most likely winner, and some see her as very likely to be eliminated deep into the merge but very explicitly prior to the endgame. Let’s talk out both sides.

The case for Kristin as a winner is pretty clear and many in the community are making it, perhaps most prominently RHAP’s Shannon Guss. No one on the show has gotten more consistently positive content, and you could argue that a few times, the show even distorted the truth to make her content even more positive. For example, she was shown dunking on Kilby during the negotiation, even though anecdotal evidence later told us she didn’t necessarily get better supplies. That’s been a recurring theme. Even the negativity she’s gotten, which has mostly been from Maggie confessionals, has framed her more as dangerous than incompetent or annoying.

If you dig a little deeper, however, there is actually some cause for concern with Kristin’s edit. Many in the community think she’s being framed as a fan favorite we’re supposed to be sad about exiting the game deep into the merge, and there’s definitely some evidence for that. First, while she’s been a consistent part of the show, there are actually seven players who have more confessionals than her at this point in the game: Devin, Jelly, Lewis, Kilby, Brady, Ori and Erik. She’s only middle of the pack among the players who are left, and that’s actually really bad considering she was picked for negotiation, went to exile island, got swap screwed and got prominently injured during an episode.

Given all the plot-relevant moments she’s been involved in, it’s actually kind of weird she hasn’t gotten more content, which is probably because it keeps getting cut. An emotional scene between her and the Survivor doctor where she was informed she would be allowed to stay in the game got cut and released as an online exclusive. Another scene from this past episode where she explained what happened on Exile Island to her tribe got cut and also released as an online exclusive. Given she’s only in the middle of the pack on content, if she were the winner, it kind of feels like the show would find reasons to use her, not cut compelling scenes she’s involved in.

To me, the most likely scenario is probably that she gets taken out in the 5 to 7 range. That’s typically the point in the game where all the remaining players work together to eliminate the people they think are most likely to win a jury vote, and as a strong public speaker with great relationships, a compelling backstory and a passion for the game, Kristin screams jury threat. There’s also the pesky issue of fire hanging over her head too. We’ve been repeatedly shown and the other players have repeatedly seen her making fire very quickly. She’s the type of player you have to eliminate before the final four, which is why that range just outside makes so much sense.

I have no idea who is going to win this season (though I can guess who is going to lose) and by extension, I have no idea where Kristin is going to finish. All I know for sure is that she’s delightful, and the editors clearly want us to have positive feelings about her, whether she's the possible host Jeff Probst was referring to or not. Maybe that’s because she’s going to go on and win the whole thing, or maybe that’s because she’s the emotional gut punch we’re going to get when she’s betrayed by other players who are worried she’ll win the jury vote if she gets there.

#3686. What Overwatch Learned About Its Own Story In 2026

Overwatchâs big 2026 reboot brought in 10 new heroes and a wealth of updates ranging from gameplay tweaks to UI changes, but perhaps the most significant change is that it brought the hero shooterâs story back to the forefront. After the cancellation of Overwatch 2âs planned cooperative campaign left the gameâs already stagnant story at an unfortunate standstill, Blizzard has since committed to its longest-running singular arc through cinematics, short stories, comics, and audio dramas that have been telling the story of Vendettaâs reign as the new leader of the terrorist organization Talon.

With the release of the new animated cinematic âIn the Wolfâs Mouth,â that story has reached its conclusion. Fans are debating whether or not the Overwatch universe has moved forward in a meaningful way now that Doomfist has reclaimed his place at the top of Talon, but Blizzard has at least set a precedent establishing that it will finally tell full stories within this universe after a decade of mostly nudging things along at a glacial pace. So what has Blizzard learned in the first year of Overwatch finally having a real story?Â

In a roundtable interview with game director Aaron Keller and associate game director Alec Dawson, the pair talked about how it’s moving into the next phase of Overwatchâs narrative. The next story arc will begin with what Keller describes as “probably the best cinematic” the team has put out since Overwatch‘s launch, but he also indicated that the team hopes to do a better job ofÂ  drawing players’ attention to the story as new lore drops are released on YouTube, social media channels, and in the in-game Story menu.

âI think that it can be easy to miss some of this stuff when we release it. Like just yesterday, we released a cinematic that was like the wrap-up to the 2026 story. It was our finale. It’s this really amazing piece of this fight between Vendetta and Doomfist with Overwatch present. And sometimes I feel like unless you’re really following along, it might be easy to miss some of those pieces. So I think one of the things that we’re talking about, just like how do we get the story out in front of players to where it’s not only like a âcan’t missâ moment, but like it’s also somethingÂ  that they can’t miss because they also know about it, you know?âÂ

While visibility is one side of the coin, Keller also says the team is using this first year as a testing ground for what formats work best to tell Overwatchâs story. Currently, the team cycles through animated shorts, motion comics, and audio dramas narrated by members of the gameâs exceptional voice cast, but there are also short stories and digital comics in the mix as well, and Blizzard says it wants its next arc to be better about helping the average player piece all these disparate parts together.

âWe kind of do [story] across a lot of different medium types, and so I think sometimes that might also make it a little difficult for our players to piece some of the story elements together that we think are important,â Keller says. âSo going forward, I think we’re going to be looking at that strategy a little bit, looking at how we can like bring players up to speed a little bit, even sometimes if it’s just a sentence or two at the start of a cinematic to show that there’s been other stuff happening with the story.â

Over the past year, players have felt a bit of a disconnect between elements of the Overwatch story, as half of the narrative hasnât been featured in the game itself, but in a webcomic called Overwatch: Undivided which is found in a Webtoons digital comic app. While the cinematics and other lore drops are viewable to everyone in a readily accessible format, Undivided is on a separate app. The comic doesnât typically portray the biggest story beats on its own; it is undoubtedly supplemental material, connective tissue linking the more pivotal pieces you see in the gameâs story menu, and itâs where most of the actual Overwatch members get the most face time. It primarily follows the new generation of heroes like Juno, Wuyang, and Anran, though there are some notable interactions between members of the old crew as well, such as Reinhardt and Ana entering a romantic relationship, and Genji leaving Overwatch entirely.

So why is it separate? According to Keller, the Overwatch team had parameters in place for how each type of lore drop would portray the important moments of the gameâs story, and Undivided was meant to be more of a slice-of-life piece in between the bigger lore drops.

âWe definitely had a strategy going into the story this year, and part of it was to tell the biggest pieces of the story that we could in the cinematics and then use our big motion comics as the second piece that players ought to watch in order to be able to have a full picture of the most important parts of the story,â Keller says. âAnd then we had these other pieces, these things that internally we call âmicro stories,â where it’s several images and a narrated sort of like a story from the hero’s point of view that filled in a lot of pieces of their personality and who they were, and when you look at those pieces right there, that told the story and it gave you a lot of context on like who our new heroes were. But there was so much going on over the course of the year. And there’s so many fun things that you just want to be able to imagine or think about for our Overwatch heroes that we wanted another way to tell that. We wanted to be able to connect it all together. And that’s really where the Webtoon comes in, it does serve that purpose.

And while it will talk about some of the bigger pieces of story we have, like the attack on [Overwatch headquarters in] Gibraltar at the start of this year, it also gets to do all of these really fun moments. You get insights into who Juno is. You get to go see Reinhardt and Ana on a date, and it lets us really fill in those spaces. I think that, for us, that was the strategy of how we were going to release this story is like all of the big things you need to follow to understand it on one side in the game and in this webtoon to really fill in a lot of the other pieces and give players a chance to kind of see Overwatch in a different light.â

Whatever the format, Dawson says that one of the goals now is for every year of Overwatch story to feel like itâs building on what came before, rather than like each new story arc is some sort of self-contained thing.

âThere’s also, I think, room for us to get better at build-up to these stories and making sure that maybe the story before the previous one affects the world state in some way that leaves room for other stories to have their time in the sun,â Dawson says. âSo I think there’s making sure [thereâs] connective tissue not just within the year itself, but from arc to arc. [The story] feels like something that is cohesive to the world of Overwatch. And it’s like the whole thing changes in a way that makes this next thing possible. So, some of those stakes, I think we’re looking at, and how your relationship can change with Overwatch, but also with the heroes themselves.â

Though Vendetta has been defeated, Overwatchâs current story arc still has a handful of lore drops left before the end of the current season, which will also likely introduce a new hero colloquially known as the âOmnic Detective,â who fans have theorized may reintroduce the Null Sector storyline that was dropped when Blizzard canceled Overwatch 2âs campaign. When I asked Keller and Dawson if there were any specific lore pieces from over the years that fans should read or watch in the lead-up to the next story arc, they said they didnât want to spoil anything specific, but Keller reiterated that people might want to go back and watch some of the old cinematics, though the team is looking into a way to catch folks up on things they mightâve missed.

âI think that our old cinematics are best-in-class and they’re amazing,â he says. âAnd I’ll go back and I’ll still rewatch that âDragonsâ cinematic, you know, the story of Hanzo and Genji. I think it’s pretty incredible. And we do have a lot that are there. I guess all I would say is the story that we’re going to be telling in 2027, it is directly related to some of what people have seen in the story in Overwatch previously. It’s continuing a chapter. It’s not starting something solely from scratch. I think we’re putting together some catch-up videos for players, so hopefully they’d be able to watch some of that. But I would always welcome people to go back and check out some of the previous ones. They’re really great to watch, it wouldn’t hurt to be all caught up before we start rolling out what’s coming soon.â

Keller says that keeping Overwatch players engaged with the story has been âgratifyingâ for the team, having previously talked about how he actually enjoyed that Doomfist fans took issue with his defeat at the beginning of the year. While there have been debates among fans about the effectiveness of the Reign of Talon storyâs conclusion, Keller says the team views its new story initiative as âsuccessfulâ and plans to invest even more into the Overwatch narrative next year, with the Omnic Detectiveâs announcement cinematic acting as a âprologue.â But this is all external media and doesnât take place inside the game itself. Overwatch has implemented lore elements into maps, including new hero pre-match interactions that have heroes bantering about current events in the story, which helps flesh out the world and its heroesâ places in it. But after the original cooperative campaign fell through, is Blizzard still considering any kind of PvE element that could move the story forward alongside all these new initiatives?

Keller says that the surge of players theyâve seen hop into Overwatchâs previous PvE events was âreally big,â but they often have a âfast drop-off,â and itâs made them harder to invest in from a time and resources standpoint. Comparatively, cinematics and comics are much less resource-intensive, which has made them a more viable vehicle for Blizzard to deliver story. Since data shows players primarily engage with Overwatchâs competitive shooter side, thatâs where the team has chosen to direct its energy,Â  but does that mean that story-driven PvE content is no longer possible? âI would never discount it,â Keller says. âIt’s hard to find a designer that’s ever going to discount anything like a possibility, you know? And I think that potentially there’s a way for us to try to do something like that, but in order to do it, we have to make sure that we’re still focusing on our core game experience. That’s the most important thing for us. And so I think that there’s probably some room for some small experiences like that in Overwatch, but for anything that would be really big, really comprehensive, I think that the thing that players in their heads think, like the fantasy of what an Overwatch PvE experience would be, or especially like a story-based PvE experience would be, I think that that would just have to end up being a whole new game developed by a whole new team.â

âWe want to be doing as much of it as we can, but we still always want to be doing it in a way that's also responsibleâ

#3685. This Ultra-Wide Samsung Gaming Monitor Is $600 Off

An ultra-wide curved gaming monitor with ridiculous specs is every gamer's dream, but they (usually) don't come cheap. The 57-inch Samsung Odyssey Neo G9, one of the best ultra-wide gaming monitors on the market, is currently on sale for $1,499.99 (originally $2,499.99 at launch)—that's its second-best discount, according to price-checking tools.

The Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 Series is not a regular ultra-wide gaming monitor. It has impressive specs, but you'll need a top-notch gaming computer with specific outputs to take full advantage of its 240Hz refresh rate potential.

This monitor came out in 2023 with an "excellent" review from PCMag, mainly due to its impressive 7,680 by 2,160 4K native resolution, the ridiculous 57-inch screen size, its great color range and accuracy, the 240Hz refresh rate, and its design. The VA panel also means you get a bright 1,000-nit screen. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use a DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful modern graphics card that is able to push the frames at a native resolution to max out the monitor's potential.

Although it is pricey, this monitor is a great value for the right gamer. You'll need plenty of space to fit a 57-inch screen, as well as a powerful computer to justify using the monitor—if you're not a competitive gamer with a powerful computer, it's probably not worth the price tag. Instead, consider this Asus gaming monitor going for $329.99 (originally $499) right now.

This week, Bethesda Game Studios is celebrating its 40th birthday—a celebration that included the full name reveal of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, successfully completing the eight-year task of adding a word to a thing.

In addition, Bethesda is commemorating the occasion with the launch of a 40th anniversary site collecting the anecdotes and favorite memories of studio staff, including one Alan Nanes. Now a design director, Nanes was originally hired at Bethesda as one of its first full-time QA testers—and by his own description, he got the job by being a pleasant fellow to spend time with.

According to Nanes, his history with Bethesda started during Morrowind's development. He was close friends with Bethesda devs in multiple departments, and it was an era where that was enough to get you in the building.

"Things were a bit 'Wild West' back then, and my friends allowed me to hang out (yes, before I was an employee) there, playing multiplayer games with them and just getting to know everyone," Nanes wrote. "Eventually, Todd Howard noticed my presence in the studio and asked if I wanted to test out their new game."

In time, his impromptu testing sessions started attracting an audience of Bethesda developers who would pick his brain about their design choices, scribble notes, and debate with each other about potential tweaks to the game while watching over his shoulder.

"It was an extraordinary feeling, the first time I felt like I was contributing to the creation of an actual videogame (I believe you can find my name in the Morrowind manual's credits under 'Special Thanks')," Nanes said. "After this became a regular occurrence, Todd Howard and Ashley Cheng seemed to decide having full-time, in-studio QA would be a valuable addition to the team, and I took on that mantle."

Nanes later graduated to a quest designer position for Oblivion, and was more recently credited as lead companions designer on Starfield. But while his tenure at Bethesda might've had a storybook trajectory, the history of QA workers at the studio has been a contentious one in the years since Nanes was hired.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Driven by frustrations surrounding compensation, advancement opportunities, workload, and more, QA workers at Bethesda's parent company ZeniMax initiated a unionization vote in 2022, officially forming ZeniMax Workers United - CWA—then the largest videogame union in the US—when the vote succeeded in January 2023.

Those frustrations remained unaddressed as contract negotiations with Microsoft stalled for over two years, driving the QA union to vote overwhelmingly in favor of authorizing a strike in April 2025. Its contract was ultimately ratified in June 2025. When a number of those QA workers were affected by Xbox's July 2026 layoffs, that contract allowed the union to enter into an "effects bargaining" process to negotiate severance terms for its impacted members, culminating in "a significant agreement" in September 2026.

Every Halloween, I think I've seen the year's best celebrity costume, and then somebody comes along and changes my mind. And while there's plenty keeping me entertained on the 2026 TV schedule, former Riverdale stars Madelaine Petsch and Camila Mendes just gave me a fictional show I'd absolutely watch. Petsch and Mendes spent Halloween dressed as Wilma Flintstone and Betty Rubble, respectively, and their ridiculously glamorous photo shoot has me wishing The Real Housewives of Bedrock were an actual series I could binge.

Petsch and Mendes shared the pictures in a joint Instagram post on Halloween, captioning them "The Real Housewives of Bedrock," complete with a bone emoji. Amber Asaly shot the photos, and they look like promotional stills for the most unhinged Bravo spinoff imaginable. Prehistoric sets, dramatic side-eyes, and enough attitude suggest somebody's about to get kicked out of the Bedrock country club. Seriously, take a look:

A post shared by Madelaine Petsch (@madelame)

Since Andy Cohen recently teased the possibility of more Real Housewives cities, I think somebody should put Bedrock on the list. Seriously, who’s Flintmobile’s stone log rollers do I gotta buff to get this thing greenlit?

Petsch nails Wilma's signature look: red curls piled high, a white one-shoulder dress with a jagged hem, and those enormous pearls. Mendes, meanwhile, makes a fantastic Betty in a blue dress, matching hair bow and sleek dark bob. They've kept the recognizable Flintstones details while giving everything a glossy, fashion-editorial makeover. I'd genuinely love to see the rest of their imaginary cast.

The photos are where the joke really takes off. In one, Betty leans over to whisper something into Wilma's ear, while Wilma looks appropriately scandalized. Another pic shows them posing with champagne glasses, and there are shots of the pair lounging among rocky scenery lifted from the cartoon. They even brought two little white dogs into the mix. I'm not sure what the dogs have to do with prehistoric suburbia, I suppose its hard to secure a tiny dino on short notice, so I’m glad the pups got an invite.

As much as I love the outfits, someone in the Instagram comments deserves a gold star for the funniest response to the entire shoot. User @herecomesjoey wrote:

RIP CW, you would’ve greenlit this show by Monday morning 😭👌🏽🔥😍

I've always had a soft spot for how the 1994 live-action Flintstones movie brought Bedrock to life, and these costumes have that same wonderfully ridiculous attention to detail. Only this time, Wilma and Betty look ready for a Bravo reunion special.

They don’t really produce their own original series anymore, but the CW is still on the air, and I laughed harder than I probably should have. Considering these two spent seven seasons on Riverdale, a show that got increasingly bizarre right up through its series finale, a CW-style Flintstones drama feels almost plausible. I can already hear the trailer voice-over: "In Bedrock, everybody has something to hide."

Of course, Petsch and Mendes have a history of taking Halloween costumes very seriously. Just last year, they dressed as Kim Possible and Shego, proving that transforming into beloved cartoon characters is becoming something of an annual tradition for these two. Before that, they joined fellow Riverdale alum Lili Reinhart to dress as the Gotham City Sirens for Halloween, after previously transforming into the Sanderson sisters from Hocus Pocus. This year's costume is a duo rather than a trio, but Reinhart still showed up in the comments with a perfect one-word endorsement: "Icons." I can't argue with her.

What really sells these pictures for me is how completely the actresses commit to the bit. They look ready to feud over a dinner-party seating chart carved into a stone tablet. Unfortunately, The Real Housewives of Bedrock isn't a real series. For now, it's an excellent Halloween photo shoot and another reminder that Petsch and Mendes know how to have fun together long after Riverdale ended. But if anybody wants to commission a pilot, I expect a reunion special hosted by a particularly exhausted Fred Flintstone.

Riverdale is streaming in its entirety with a Netflix subscription.

#3682. EA Reportedly Chose An Unannounced Star Wars Game Over BioWare’s Next Mass Effect

EA recently announced it was shutting down BioWare, ending a studio responsible for multiple hit games over 30 years. According to a new report, EA's decision was driven by economics, as it had to choose between funding a new Mass Effect and backing the safer bet, Star Wars: Battlefront 3.

Bloomberg's Jason Schreier reported that EA had to choose between two costly projects, and with the added pressure of paying off $18 billion in leveraged debt after its sale to a business consortium and Saudi Arabia's investment fund, Battlefront 3 made more financial sense. To add insult to injury, Battlefront 3 isn't even in development yet, and it hasn't been officially announced.

"They chose to invest in Star Wars and shut down BioWare as a result, said the people familiar, speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to talk to the press," Schreier wrote. "Star Wars: Battlefront 3 has not even begun development yet, but EA executives saw it as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect--and the publisher behind Battlefield has always been more comfortable with shooters than RPGs."

Schreier added that "corporate politics" may have also influenced the decision, as one of the studio's key advocates, senior EA exec Laura Miele, was reportedly sidelined when EA Sports veterans David Tinson and Cam Weber were promoted. BioWare also experienced several flops over the last decade, with Mass Effect: Andromeda, Anthem, and Dragon Age: The Veilguard failing to meet sales expectations, which further influenced EA's decision to shut down the studio.

After BioWare's closure, more details on its Mass Effect project have emerged. A trailer for Mass Effect: Universe was posted online last week; the game's details made it sound like a sci-fi version of John Wick, and video game composer Austin Wintory shared an experimental score as part of his Mass Effect audition tape.
